content.title: Week 15, day 3: Construct a proof
content.markdown: You are in **MPSI S1**. This page follows the week 15 syllabus requirement: Polynomial division, gcd, and partial fractions.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can write a complete proof of this exact target: prove that a polynomial has a repeated root exactly when it shares a nonconstant gcd with its derivative.

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Prove that a polynomial has a repeated root exactly when it shares a nonconstant gcd with its derivative.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: $\alpha$ is a root of $P$ exactly when $P(\alpha)=0$, equivalently when $x-\alpha$ divides $P$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 14: Elementary row operations preserve the set of solutions of a linear system. Week 12: A solution of a differential equation is a function defined on the stated interval whose derivatives satisfy the equation at every point. Week 7: A subsequence has the form $(u_{\varphi(n)})$ where $\varphi$ is strictly increasing. A cluster value is a limit of some convergent subsequence. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove that a polynomial has a repeated root exactly when it shares a nonconstant gcd with its derivative.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a nonzero polynomial cannot have more roots than its degree

We argue by induction on the degree. A nonzero constant has no root. Now let $P$ have degree $d\ge1$. If $P$ has no root, the claim is immediate. If $a$ is a root, polynomial division gives $P=(X-a)Q$ with $\deg Q=d-1$.

Every root of $P$ other than $a$ is a root of $Q$. By the induction hypothesis, $Q$ has at most $d-1$ roots, so $P$ has at most $d$ roots.

**Why the proof is complete.** It separates the no-root case, uses factorization at one chosen root, and reduces the degree before invoking induction.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** $\alpha$ is a root of $P$ exactly when $P(\alpha)=0$, equivalently when $x-\alpha$ divides $P$.

**Worked example to compare:** $2$ is a root of $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$.

**Boundary to compare:** A degree-$d$ nonzero polynomial has at most $d$ distinct roots; the zero polynomial is the exceptional case.

### Week 14 — Matrices · Gaussian elimination

**Definition.** Gaussian elimination uses row swaps, nonzero row scaling, and row replacement to reach an equivalent echelon system.

**Example.** Replacing $R_2$ by $R_2-2R_1$ preserves the solution set.

**Boundary.** A row may not be divided by an expression unless it is known to be nonzero.

**Proof target.** Prove that replacing one equation by itself plus a multiple of another preserves the solution set.

**Decisive proof route.** Replacing $E_i$ by $E_i+\lambda E_j$ does not change any common solution because a solution of the old equations satisfies the new one. Conversely, subtracting $\lambda E_j$ recovers $E_i$, so every solution of the new system solves the old one.

### Week 12 — Differential equations · First-order linear equations

**Definition.** A first-order linear equation $y'+a(x)y=b(x)$ is solved by an integrating factor on an interval where the coefficients are continuous.

**Example.** For $y'+y=1$, the solutions are $y(x)=1+Ce^{-x}$.

**Boundary.** Dividing by a coefficient that can vanish changes the equation and may lose solutions.

**Proof target.** Prove that the difference of two solutions of the same inhomogeneous linear equation solves the homogeneous equation.

**Decisive proof route.** If $L[y_1]=g$ and $L[y_2]=g$ for a linear differential operator $L$, then linearity gives $L[y_1-y_2]=L[y_1]-L[y_2]=0$. Thus the difference solves the homogeneous equation.

### Week 7 — Sequences · Cluster values

**Definition.** A cluster value of a sequence is the limit of at least one convergent subsequence.

**Example.** For $u_n=(-1)^n$, the cluster values are $-1$ and $1$.

**Boundary.** A value approached by finitely many terms only is not a cluster value.

**Proof target.** Prove that every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit.

**Decisive proof route.** Let $u_n\to\ell$ and let $u_{n_k}$ be a subsequence. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ with $n\ge N\Rightarrow|u_n-\ell|<\varepsilon$. Since $n_k\ge k$, every $k\ge N$ also satisfies $|u_{n_k}-\ell|<\varepsilon$.

content.markdown: You are in **MPSI S1**. This page follows the week 16 syllabus requirement: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can state the defining conditions for Vector spaces · Space, verify the supplied example, and identify why the boundary case fails.

## Why this matters

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms over a stated field. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 15: Euclidean division writes $A=BQ+R$ with $\deg R<\deg B$ when $B\ne0$. Week 13: For integers $a,b$, $a$ divides $b$ when $b=ak$ for some integer $k$. The greatest common divisor is the positive common divisor divisible by every other common divisor. Week 8: A function is continuous at $a$ when $f(x)$ approaches $f(a)$ whenever $x$ approaches $a$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Define the objects in vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums

A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms over a stated field.

### A complete first example

The real polynomials of degree at most $3$ form a four-dimensional real vector space.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

The polynomials of degree exactly $3$ do not form a vector space because they do not contain zero.

content.markdown: You are in **MPSI S1**. This page follows the week 16 syllabus requirement: Vector spaces, subspaces, sums, and direct sums.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can apply a definition-first method to a complete Vector spaces · Subspace verification and check its boundary.

## Why this matters

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A subset is a subspace when it contains zero and is closed under all linear combinations. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 15: Euclidean division writes $A=BQ+R$ with $\deg R<\deg B$ when $B\ne0$. Week 13: For integers $a,b$, $a$ divides $b$ when $b=ak$ for some integer $k$. The greatest common divisor is the positive common divisor divisible by every other common divisor. Week 8: A function is continuous at $a$ when $f(x)$ approaches $f(a)$ whenever $x$ approaches $a$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Vector spaces · Subspace

A subset is a subspace when it contains zero and is closed under all linear combinations.

### Complete worked problem

Prove that $F=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x+y+z=0\}$ is a vector subspace of $\mathbb R^3$.

### Complete worked derivation

The zero vector belongs to $F$ because $0+0+0=0$. Take $u=(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $v=(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ in $F$, and let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$. Then

$$\alpha(x_1+y_1+z_1)+\beta(x_2+y_2+z_2)=0.$$

This is the sum of the coordinates of $\alpha u+\beta v$, so $\alpha u+\beta v\in F$. The set contains zero and is closed under every linear combination; therefore it is a subspace.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

The parallel plane $x+y+z=1$ does not contain the zero vector and is not closed under scalar multiplication. It is an affine set, not a vector subspace.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove that $E=F\oplus G$ exactly when every vector has a unique decomposition $f+g$.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: the kernel of a linear map is a subspace

Let $T:E\to F$ be linear. We prove that $\ker T$ is a vector subspace of $E$.

First, $T(0_E)=0_F$, so $0_E\in\ker T$. Now take $x,y\in\ker T$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$. By linearity,

$$T(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha T(x)+\beta T(y)=0_F.$$

Thus $\alpha x+\beta y\in\ker T$. The kernel contains zero and is closed under linear combinations, so it is a subspace.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** We stated the ambient spaces, then checked exactly the two subspace obligations. Each equality cites linearity before using the kernel assumptions.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** $V=E\oplus F$ means every $v\in V$ has a unique decomposition $v=e+f$ with $e\in E$ and $f\in F$.

**Worked example to compare:** $\mathbb R^2=\operatorname{span}(e_1)\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_2)$.

**Boundary to compare:** The condition $E+F=V$ is not enough; uniqueness also requires $E\cap F=\{0\}$.

### Week 15 — Polynomials · Roots

**Definition.** $\alpha$ is a root of $P$ exactly when $P(\alpha)=0$, equivalently when $x-\alpha$ divides $P$.

**Example.** $2$ is a root of $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$.

**Boundary.** A degree-$d$ nonzero polynomial has at most $d$ distinct roots; the zero polynomial is the exceptional case.

**Proof target.** Prove that a polynomial has a repeated root exactly when it shares a nonconstant gcd with its derivative.

**Decisive proof route.** A repeated root $a$ makes both $P(a)$ and $P'(a)$ zero, so $X-a$ divides their gcd. Conversely, if a nonconstant gcd has a root $a$, then $P(a)=P'(a)=0$, and factoring $P=(X-a)Q$ gives $Q(a)=0$, hence $(X-a)^2\mid P$.

### Week 13 — Integer arithmetic · Bézout identity

**Definition.** Bézout's identity states that $\gcd(a,b)$ is an integer combination $ua+vb$.

**Example.** $\gcd(30,18)=6=(-1)30+2\cdot18$.

**Boundary.** The equation $ua+vb=1$ is possible exactly when $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

**Proof target.** Prove Euclid's lemma from Bézout's identity.

**Decisive proof route.** If $p\mid ab$ and $\gcd(p,a)=1$, choose $u,v$ with $up+va=1$. Multiplying by $b$ gives $b=upb+vab$, and both terms are divisible by $p$, so $p\mid b$.

### Week 8 — Real functions · Intermediate value theorem

**Definition.** A continuous real function on an interval takes every value between any two of its values.

**Example.** Since $x^3-x-1$ changes sign between $1$ and $2$, it has a root in $(1,2)$.

**Boundary.** The intermediate value theorem gives existence, not uniqueness, and requires continuity on the full interval.

**Proof target.** Prove that a continuous function with opposite signs at the endpoints has a zero between them.

**Decisive proof route.** For continuous $f$ on $[a,b]$ with $f(a)f(b)\le0$, the intermediate value theorem applies because zero lies between the endpoint values. Hence some $c\in[a,b]$ satisfies $f(c)=0$; strict opposite signs place $c$ in $(a,b)$.

### Week 15 — Polynomials · Roots

**Definition.** $\alpha$ is a root of $P$ exactly when $P(\alpha)=0$, equivalently when $x-\alpha$ divides $P$.

**Example.** $2$ is a root of $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$.

**Boundary.** A degree-$d$ nonzero polynomial has at most $d$ distinct roots; the zero polynomial is the exceptional case.

**Proof target.** Prove that a polynomial has a repeated root exactly when it shares a nonconstant gcd with its derivative.

**Decisive proof route.** A repeated root $a$ makes both $P(a)$ and $P'(a)$ zero, so $X-a$ divides their gcd. Conversely, if a nonconstant gcd has a root $a$, then $P(a)=P'(a)=0$, and factoring $P=(X-a)Q$ gives $Q(a)=0$, hence $(X-a)^2\mid P$.

**Definition.** Bézout's identity states that $\gcd(a,b)$ is an integer combination $ua+vb$.

**Example.** $\gcd(30,18)=6=(-1)30+2\cdot18$.

**Boundary.** The equation $ua+vb=1$ is possible exactly when $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

**Proof target.** Prove Euclid's lemma from Bézout's identity.

**Definition.** A continuous real function on an interval takes every value between any two of its values.

**Example.** Since $x^3-x-1$ changes sign between $1$ and $2$, it has a root in $(1,2)$.

**Boundary.** The intermediate value theorem gives existence, not uniqueness, and requires continuity on the full interval.

**Proof target.** Prove that a continuous function with opposite signs at the endpoints has a zero between them.

**Decisive proof route.** For continuous $f$ on $[a,b]$ with $f(a)f(b)\le0$, the intermediate value theorem applies because zero lies between the endpoint values. Hence some $c\in[a,b]$ satisfies $f(c)=0$; strict opposite signs place $c$ in $(a,b)$.

### Exact definition or theorem: Linear maps · Kernel

$\ker T=\{v:T(v)=0\}$ is the subspace of inputs annihilated by a linear map.

### Complete worked problem

For the linear map $T:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ defined by $T(x,y,z)=(x+y,y+z)$, determine a basis of $\ker T$.

### Complete worked derivation

A vector lies in the kernel exactly when

$$x+y=0,\qquad y+z=0.$$

Thus $x=-y$ and $z=-y$. Writing $y=t$ gives

$$(x,y,z)=t(-1,1,-1).$$

Every such vector maps to $(0,0)$, and every kernel vector has this form. Therefore

$$\ker T=\operatorname{span}\{(-1,1,-1)\},$$

so $(-1,1,-1)$ is a basis of the kernel.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

The kernel is a subset of the domain $\mathbb R^3$. The zero vector in the codomain is the value being pulled back; it is not itself the kernel.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

### Complete model proof: the kernel of a linear map is a subspace

Let $T:E\to F$ be linear. We prove that $\ker T$ is a vector subspace of $E$.

Thus $\alpha x+\beta y\in\ker T$. The kernel contains zero and is closed under linear combinations, so it is a subspace.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** The rank of a linear map is the dimension of its image.

**Worked example to compare:** The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ has rank $1$ because its columns span one line.

**Boundary to compare:** Rank is not the number of nonzero entries or nonzero rows before elimination.

### Week 16 — Vector spaces · Direct sums

**Definition.** $V=E\oplus F$ means every $v\in V$ has a unique decomposition $v=e+f$ with $e\in E$ and $f\in F$.

**Example.** $\mathbb R^2=\operatorname{span}(e_1)\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_2)$.

**Boundary.** The condition $E+F=V$ is not enough; uniqueness also requires $E\cap F=\{0\}$.

**Proof target.** Prove that $E=F\oplus G$ exactly when every vector has a unique decomposition $f+g$.

**Decisive proof route.** If $E=F\oplus G$, existence comes from $E=F+G$ and uniqueness from $F\cap G=\{0\}$. Conversely, unique decompositions imply every vector lies in $F+G$, and a vector in $F\cap G$ has decompositions $v+0=0+v$, so it must be zero.

### Week 14 — Matrices · Gaussian elimination

**Definition.** Gaussian elimination uses row swaps, nonzero row scaling, and row replacement to reach an equivalent echelon system.

**Example.** Replacing $R_2$ by $R_2-2R_1$ preserves the solution set.

**Boundary.** A row may not be divided by an expression unless it is known to be nonzero.

**Proof target.** Prove that replacing one equation by itself plus a multiple of another preserves the solution set.

**Decisive proof route.** Replacing $E_i$ by $E_i+\lambda E_j$ does not change any common solution because a solution of the old equations satisfies the new one. Conversely, subtracting $\lambda E_j$ recovers $E_i$, so every solution of the new system solves the old one.

### Week 9 — Real functions · Mean value theorem

**Definition.** The mean value theorem gives $f'(c)=[f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$ under continuity and differentiability hypotheses.

**Example.** Applied to $f(x)=x^2$ on $[1,3]$, it gives $2c=4$, hence $c=2$.

**Boundary.** The theorem identifies at least one point; it does not say the derivative is constant.

**Proof target.** Derive the monotonicity criterion from the mean-value theorem.

**Decisive proof route.** If $f'\ge0$ on an interval and $x<y$, the mean-value theorem gives $f(y)-f(x)=f'(c)(y-x)\ge0$, so $f$ is nondecreasing. The strict version follows from $f'>0$.

### Week 1 — Finite calculations · Finite sums and products

**Definition.** A finite sum $\sum_{k=p}^{q}u_k$ adds one term for each integer index from $p$ through $q$; a finite product $\prod_{k=p}^{q}u_k$ multiplies those terms. A telescoping sum is rewritten so all non-boundary terms cancel in matched pairs.

**Example.** $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k-(k-1))=(1-0)+(2-1)+\cdots+(n-(n-1))=n$ for every integer $n\ge1$.

**Boundary.** In $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k-(k-2))$, the terms do not cancel in consecutive opposite pairs, so deleting all interior terms would be invalid.

**Proof target.** Prove by induction that $1+\cdots+n=n(n+1)/2$.

**Decisive proof route.** For $n=1$, both sides equal $1$. If $1+\cdots+n=n(n+1)/2$, then adding $n+1$ gives $n(n+1)/2+n+1=(n+1)(n+2)/2$. Induction proves the formula for every $n\ge1$.

**Definition.** A finite sum $\sum_{k=p}^{q}u_k$ adds one term for each integer index from $p$ through $q$; a finite product $\prod_{k=p}^{q}u_k$ multiplies those terms. A telescoping sum is rewritten so all non-boundary terms cancel in matched pairs.

**Example.** $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k-(k-1))=(1-0)+(2-1)+\cdots+(n-(n-1))=n$ for every integer $n\ge1$.

**Boundary.** In $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k-(k-2))$, the terms do not cancel in consecutive opposite pairs, so deleting all interior terms would be invalid.

**Proof target.** Prove by induction that $1+\cdots+n=n(n+1)/2$.

**Decisive proof route.** For $n=1$, both sides equal $1$. If $1+\cdots+n=n(n+1)/2$, then adding $n+1$ gives $n(n+1)/2+n+1=(n+1)(n+2)/2$. Induction proves the formula for every $n\ge1$.

## Why this matters

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A change-of-basis matrix converts coordinate columns between two ordered bases; an endomorphism matrix changes by similarity. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 17: A linear map preserves sums and scalar multiples. Its kernel contains inputs sent to zero; its image contains all outputs reached. Week 15: Euclidean division writes $A=BQ+R$ with $\deg R<\deg B$ when $B\ne0$. Week 10: A function is convex when its graph lies below every chord joining two points of the graph. Week 2: On the unit circle, the point at angle $x$ has coordinates $(\cos x,\sin x)$. Periodicity and symmetries follow from this geometric definition. ## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Linear maps · Change of basis

A change-of-basis matrix converts coordinate columns between two ordered bases; an endomorphism matrix changes by similarity.

### Complete worked problem

Let $T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ have matrix $A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$ in the standard basis. Find its matrix in the ordered basis $b_1=(1,1)$, $b_2=(1,-1)$.

### Complete worked derivation

The change-of-basis matrix whose columns are the new basis vectors in standard coordinates is

$$P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad P^{-1}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Because the same basis is changed in the domain and codomain, the new matrix is

$$P^{-1}AP=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3/2&1/2\\1/2&3/2\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its first column also equals the new coordinates of $T(b_1)=(2,1)$, which checks the direction of the conversion.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Using $PAP^{-1}$ instead would reverse the coordinate conversion. Similarity uses $P^{-1}AP$ when $P$ sends new coordinate columns to old coordinate columns.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove that the matrix of the identity map between two bases is invertible.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: the kernel of a linear map is a subspace

Let $T:E\to F$ be linear. We prove that $\ker T$ is a vector subspace of $E$.

First, $T(0_E)=0_F$, so $0_E\in\ker T$. Now take $x,y\in\ker T$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$. By linearity,

$$T(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha T(x)+\beta T(y)=0_F.$$

Thus $\alpha x+\beta y\in\ker T$. The kernel contains zero and is closed under linear combinations, so it is a subspace.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** We stated the ambient spaces, then checked exactly the two subspace obligations. Each equality cites linearity before using the kernel assumptions.

Week 15: Euclidean division writes $A=BQ+R$ with $\deg R<\deg B$ when $B\ne0$. Week 10: A function is convex when its graph lies below every chord joining two points of the graph. ## Use the feedback

Read the earliest important issue first. Rewrite that step before continuing. Keep every part that the review identifies as correct.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** The matrix of a linear map records the coordinates of the images of basis vectors in chosen domain and codomain bases.

**Worked example to compare:** The columns of the standard matrix of $T(x,y)=(x+y,y)$ are $(1,0)^T$ and $(1,1)^T$.

**Boundary to compare:** A matrix represents a map only after the two bases and their order are fixed.

### Week 17 — Linear maps · Linear maps

**Definition.** $T:V\to W$ is linear when $T(ax+by)=aT(x)+bT(y)$ for all vectors and scalars.

**Example.** $T(x,y)=(x+y,y)$ is a linear map on $\mathbb R^2$.

**Boundary.** The map $x\mapsto x+1$ is affine, not linear, because it does not send zero to zero.

**Proof target.** Prove that the kernel and image of a linear map are subspaces.

**Decisive proof route.** For a linear map $T:E\to F$, $0\in\ker T$ and $T(\alpha x+\beta y)=0$ for kernel vectors, so the kernel is a subspace. The image contains zero and is closed because $\alpha T(x)+\beta T(y)=T(\alpha x+\beta y)$.

### Week 15 — Polynomials · Roots

**Definition.** $\alpha$ is a root of $P$ exactly when $P(\alpha)=0$, equivalently when $x-\alpha$ divides $P$.

**Example.** $2$ is a root of $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$.

**Boundary.** A degree-$d$ nonzero polynomial has at most $d$ distinct roots; the zero polynomial is the exceptional case.

**Proof target.** Prove that a polynomial has a repeated root exactly when it shares a nonconstant gcd with its derivative.

**Decisive proof route.** A repeated root $a$ makes both $P(a)$ and $P'(a)$ zero, so $X-a$ divides their gcd. Conversely, if a nonconstant gcd has a root $a$, then $P(a)=P'(a)=0$, and factoring $P=(X-a)Q$ gives $Q(a)=0$, hence $(X-a)^2\mid P$.

### Week 10 — Real functions · Convexity

**Definition.** $f$ is convex on an interval when $f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)$ for $0\le t\le1$.

**Example.** $x\mapsto x^2$ is convex because its graph lies below every chord.

**Boundary.** A nonnegative derivative gives monotonicity, not convexity; convexity concerns how slopes change.

**Proof target.** Prove the tangent inequality for a differentiable convex function.

**Decisive proof route.** For differentiable convex $f$, the secant slopes from $x$ to $x+h$ are monotone as $h\downarrow0$. Their limit is $f'(x)$, yielding $(f(y)-f(x))/(y-x)\ge f'(x)$ and hence $f(y)\ge f(x)+f'(x)(y-x)$.

### Week 2 — Trigonometry · Identities

**Definition.** A trigonometric identity is an equality valid for every angle in its stated domain and is derived from geometric or algebraic definitions, not from a few numerical checks.

**Example.** The unit-circle equation gives $\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1$ for every real $x$.

**Boundary.** $\sqrt{1-\sin^2x}=\cos x$ fails when $\cos x<0$; the square root equals $|\cos x|$.

**Proof target.** Derive the cosine addition formula from the dot product of two unit vectors.

**Decisive proof route.** Represent the unit vectors at angles $a$ and $b$ as $(\cos a,\sin a)$ and $(\cos b,\sin b)$. Their dot product is $\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b$, but rotational invariance says it is $\cos(a-b)$. Replacing $b$ by $-b$ gives $\cos(a+b)=\cos a\cos b-\sin a\sin b$.

content.title: Week 19, day 1: Build the foundation
content.markdown: You are in **MPSI S2**. This page follows the week 19 syllabus requirement: Groups, rings, fields, and morphisms.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can state the defining conditions for Algebra · Group, verify the supplied example, and identify why the boundary case fails.

## Why this matters

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A group has an associative operation, an identity, and an inverse for every element. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 18: A basis gives each vector a unique coordinate column. A change-of-basis matrix converts coordinate columns, not the underlying vector. Week 16: A subset $F$ of a vector space is a subspace when it contains $0$ and is closed under linear combinations. Week 11: A Taylor expansion separates a function into a polynomial determined by derivatives and a remainder smaller than the last retained scale. Week 3: For $z=x+iy$, its conjugate is $\bar z=x-iy$ and $z\bar z=|z|^2=x^2+y^2$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Define the objects in groups, rings, fields, and morphisms

A group has an associative operation, an identity, and an inverse for every element.

### A complete first example

$(\mathbb Z,+)$ is a group with identity $0$ and inverse $-n$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

$(\mathbb N,+)$ is not a group because positive integers lack additive inverses in $\mathbb N$.

## Why this matters

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A ring has an abelian addition and an associative multiplication linked by distributivity. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 18: A basis gives each vector a unique coordinate column. A change-of-basis matrix converts coordinate columns, not the underlying vector. Week 16: A subset $F$ of a vector space is a subspace when it contains $0$ and is closed under linear combinations. Week 11: A Taylor expansion separates a function into a polynomial determined by derivatives and a remainder smaller than the last retained scale. Week 3: For $z=x+iy$, its conjugate is $\bar z=x-iy$ and $z\bar z=|z|^2=x^2+y^2$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Algebra · Ring

A ring has an abelian addition and an associative multiplication linked by distributivity.

### Complete worked problem

In the ring $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$, show concretely that cancellation under multiplication can fail even when the cancelled factor is nonzero.

### Complete worked derivation

The classes $[1]$ and $[4]$ are distinct modulo $6$, and $[2]$ is nonzero. Nevertheless,

$$[2][1]=[2],\qquad [2][4]=[8]=[2].$$

Thus $[2][1]=[2][4]$ while $[1]\ne[4]$. The ring axioms guarantee associative multiplication and distributivity, but they do not require every nonzero element to have a multiplicative inverse. Here $[2][3]=[0]$, so $[2]$ is a zero divisor and cannot be cancelled.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Cancellation by a nonzero factor is valid in an integral domain or by a unit, not in an arbitrary ring. Treating every nonzero residue class as invertible would incorrectly turn $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ into a field.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

content.markdown: You are in **MPSI S2**. This page follows the week 20 syllabus requirement: Permutations and determinants.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can state the defining conditions for Permutations · Cycles, verify the supplied example, and identify why the boundary case fails.

## Why this matters

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: Every permutation decomposes into disjoint cycles, unique up to cycle order and cyclic rotation. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 19: An algebraic structure is a set with operations satisfying named axioms. A morphism preserves the relevant operations. Week 17: A linear map preserves sums and scalar multiples. Its kernel contains inputs sent to zero; its image contains all outputs reached. Week 12: A solution of a differential equation is a function defined on the stated interval whose derivatives satisfy the equation at every point. Week 4: A nonzero complex number has a polar form $re^{i\theta}$ with $r>0$; its argument is defined modulo $2\pi$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Define the objects in permutations and determinants

Every permutation decomposes into disjoint cycles, unique up to cycle order and cyclic rotation.

### A complete first example

$(1\ 3\ 2)(4\ 5)$ sends $1$ to $3$, $3$ to $2$, and swaps $4,5$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

Composition order matters; permutation products are generally not commutative.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can apply a definition-first method to a complete Determinants · Multilinear verification and check its boundary.

## Why this matters

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear function of the columns that equals $1$ on the standard basis. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 19: An algebraic structure is a set with operations satisfying named axioms. A morphism preserves the relevant operations. Week 17: A linear map preserves sums and scalar multiples. Its kernel contains inputs sent to zero; its image contains all outputs reached. Week 12: A solution of a differential equation is a function defined on the stated interval whose derivatives satisfy the equation at every point. Week 4: A nonzero complex number has a polar form $re^{i\theta}$ with $r>0$; its argument is defined modulo $2\pi$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Determinants · Multilinear

The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear function of the columns that equals $1$ on the standard basis.

### Complete worked problem

Let $u=(1,3)$ and $v=(2,-1)$. Use alternating multilinearity, rather than a fresh determinant expansion, to compute $\det(u+2v,v)$.

### Complete worked derivation

Linearity in the first column gives

$$\det(u+2v,v)=\det(u,v)+2\det(v,v).$$

Alternation makes $\det(v,v)=0$, so the value is $\det(u,v)$. In standard coordinates,

$$\det(u,v)=\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\3&-1\end{vmatrix}=-1-6=-7.$$

Therefore $\det(u+2v,v)=-7$. Directly, $u+2v=(5,1)$ and $\det((5,1),(2,-1))=-5-2=-7$, which checks the calculation.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Multilinearity applies one column at a time. Replacing both columns simultaneously and expanding as though the determinant were linear in the pair omits cross terms and is not a valid use of the theorem.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

### Week 19 — Algebra · Morphism

**Definition.** A morphism preserves the operations and distinguished elements of the algebraic structures involved.

**Example.** Evaluation $P\mapsto P(a)$ is a ring morphism from $K[x]$ to $K$.

**Boundary.** A function between groups is not a homomorphism merely because it is bijective.

**Proof target.** Prove that the kernel of a group morphism is a normal subgroup.

**Decisive proof route.** If $x\in\ker\varphi$ and $g$ lies in the group, then $\varphi(gxg^{-1})=\varphi(g)e\varphi(g)^{-1}=e$. Thus the kernel is stable under conjugation and is normal.

### Week 17 — Linear maps · Linear maps

**Definition.** $T:V\to W$ is linear when $T(ax+by)=aT(x)+bT(y)$ for all vectors and scalars.

**Example.** $T(x,y)=(x+y,y)$ is a linear map on $\mathbb R^2$.

**Boundary.** The map $x\mapsto x+1$ is affine, not linear, because it does not send zero to zero.

**Proof target.** Prove that the kernel and image of a linear map are subspaces.

**Decisive proof route.** For a linear map $T:E\to F$, $0\in\ker T$ and $T(\alpha x+\beta y)=0$ for kernel vectors, so the kernel is a subspace. The image contains zero and is closed because $\alpha T(x)+\beta T(y)=T(\alpha x+\beta y)$.

### Week 12 — Differential equations · First-order linear equations

**Definition.** A first-order linear equation $y'+a(x)y=b(x)$ is solved by an integrating factor on an interval where the coefficients are continuous.

**Example.** For $y'+y=1$, the solutions are $y(x)=1+Ce^{-x}$.

**Boundary.** Dividing by a coefficient that can vanish changes the equation and may lose solutions.

**Proof target.** Prove that the difference of two solutions of the same inhomogeneous linear equation solves the homogeneous equation.

**Decisive proof route.** If $L[y_1]=g$ and $L[y_2]=g$ for a linear differential operator $L$, then linearity gives $L[y_1-y_2]=L[y_1]-L[y_2]=0$. Thus the difference solves the homogeneous equation.

### Week 4 — Complex numbers · Polar

**Definition.** Every nonzero complex number has the form $z=re^{i\theta}$ with $r>0$; its arguments are the numbers $\theta+2k\pi$.

**Example.** $-i=1\cdot e^{-i\pi/2}$, and $3e^{i\pi/4}$ has modulus $3$ and argument $\pi/4$ modulo $2\pi$.

**Boundary.** Zero has no argument, and a nonzero number does not have one unique argument without a chosen branch.

**Proof target.** Prove that the $n$th roots of unity form the vertices of a regular polygon.

**Decisive proof route.** The solutions of $z^n=1$ are $e^{2\pi i k/n}$ for $k=0,\ldots,n-1$. Their moduli are one and their arguments differ successively by $2\pi/n$, so they are equally spaced vertices of a regular $n$-gon.

- **Week 17 — Linear maps · Linear maps:** state the definition, reconstruct a proof of “Prove that the kernel and image of a linear map are subspaces.”, and name one hypothesis or boundary that would invalidate the argument.
- **Week 12 — Differential equations · First-order linear equations:** state the definition, reconstruct a proof of “Prove that the difference of two solutions of the same inhomogeneous linear equation solves the homogeneous equation.”, and name one hypothesis or boundary that would invalidate the argument.
- **Week 4 — Complex numbers · Polar:** state the definition, reconstruct a proof of “Prove that the $n$th roots of unity form the vertices of a regular polygon.”, and name one hypothesis or boundary that would invalidate the argument. Classify one likely error and repair the earliest invalid step.

## Task-specific reference for Permutations · Signature

**Definition.** The signature is the homomorphism from the symmetric group to $\{\pm1\}$ that assigns $-1$ to a transposition.

**Valid case.** A $k$-cycle has signature $(-1)^{k-1}$.

**Boundary.** The number of transpositions in a decomposition is not unique, but its parity is.

**Scheduled review answer key.**

### Week 19 — Algebra · Morphism

**Definition.** A morphism preserves the operations and distinguished elements of the algebraic structures involved.

**Example.** Evaluation $P\mapsto P(a)$ is a ring morphism from $K[x]$ to $K$.

**Boundary.** A function between groups is not a homomorphism merely because it is bijective.

**Proof target.** Prove that the kernel of a group morphism is a normal subgroup.

**Decisive proof route.** If $x\in\ker\varphi$ and $g$ lies in the group, then $\varphi(gxg^{-1})=\varphi(g)e\varphi(g)^{-1}=e$. Thus the kernel is stable under conjugation and is normal.

### Week 17 — Linear maps · Linear maps

**Definition.** $T:V\to W$ is linear when $T(ax+by)=aT(x)+bT(y)$ for all vectors and scalars.

**Example.** $T(x,y)=(x+y,y)$ is a linear map on $\mathbb R^2$.

**Boundary.** The map $x\mapsto x+1$ is affine, not linear, because it does not send zero to zero.

**Proof target.** Prove that the kernel and image of a linear map are subspaces.

**Decisive proof route.** For a linear map $T:E\to F$, $0\in\ker T$ and $T(\alpha x+\beta y)=0$ for kernel vectors, so the kernel is a subspace. The image contains zero and is closed because $\alpha T(x)+\beta T(y)=T(\alpha x+\beta y)$.

### Week 12 — Differential equations · First-order linear equations

**Definition.** A first-order linear equation $y'+a(x)y=b(x)$ is solved by an integrating factor on an interval where the coefficients are continuous.

**Example.** For $y'+y=1$, the solutions are $y(x)=1+Ce^{-x}$.

**Boundary.** Dividing by a coefficient that can vanish changes the equation and may lose solutions.

**Proof target.** Prove that the difference of two solutions of the same inhomogeneous linear equation solves the homogeneous equation.

**Decisive proof route.** If $L[y_1]=g$ and $L[y_2]=g$ for a linear differential operator $L$, then linearity gives $L[y_1-y_2]=L[y_1]-L[y_2]=0$. Thus the difference solves the homogeneous equation.

### Week 4 — Complex numbers · Polar

**Definition.** Every nonzero complex number has the form $z=re^{i\theta}$ with $r>0$; its arguments are the numbers $\theta+2k\pi$.

**Example.** $-i=1\cdot e^{-i\pi/2}$, and $3e^{i\pi/4}$ has modulus $3$ and argument $\pi/4$ modulo $2\pi$.

**Boundary.** Zero has no argument, and a nonzero number does not have one unique argument without a chosen branch.

**Proof target.** Prove that the $n$th roots of unity form the vertices of a regular polygon.

**Decisive proof route.** The solutions of $z^n=1$ are $e^{2\pi i k/n}$ for $k=0,\ldots,n-1$. Their moduli are one and their arguments differ successively by $2\pi/n$, so they are equally spaced vertices of a regular $n$-gon.

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: $f(x)=o(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $f(x)/g(x)\to0$ wherever the quotient is defined near $a$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 20: The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear form on columns that equals $1$ on the standard basis. Week 18: A basis gives each vector a unique coordinate column. A change-of-basis matrix converts coordinate columns, not the underlying vector. Week 13: For integers $a,b$, $a$ divides $b$ when $b=ak$ for some integer $k$. The greatest common divisor is the positive common divisor divisible by every other common divisor. Week 5: The supremum of a nonempty set bounded above is its least upper bound: it bounds the set, and no smaller number does. ## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Asymptotic comparison · Little-o notation

$f(x)=o(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $f(x)/g(x)\to0$ wherever the quotient is defined near $a$.

### Complete worked problem

Prove that $x^3=o(x^2)$ as $x\to0$, using the quotient definition and stating where the quotient is defined.

### Complete worked derivation

For $x\ne0$, the quotient of the proposed smaller term by the comparison scale is

$$\frac{x^3}{x^2}=x.$$

As $x\to0$ through nonzero values, this quotient tends to $0$. By the definition of little-o, this proves $x^3=o(x^2)$ as $x\to0$. The quotient need not be defined at the limiting point; it must be defined on a punctured neighborhood where the limit is taken.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

The relation $x^2=O(x^2)$ is true, but $x^2\ne o(x^2)$ because the quotient is constantly $1$, not a function tending to zero. Big-O boundedness is strictly weaker than little-o.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

## Today's learning goal

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Prove that equivalence is transitive.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: $f(x)=O(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $|f(x)|\le C|g(x)|$ near $a$ for some constant $C>0$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 20: The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear form on columns that equals $1$ on the standard basis. Week 18: A basis gives each vector a unique coordinate column. A change-of-basis matrix converts coordinate columns, not the underlying vector. Week 13: For integers $a,b$, $a$ divides $b$ when $b=ak$ for some integer $k$. The greatest common divisor is the positive common divisor divisible by every other common divisor. Week 5: The supremum of a nonempty set bounded above is its least upper bound: it bounds the set, and no smaller number does. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove that equivalence is transitive.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

## Use the feedback

Read the earliest important issue first. Rewrite that step before continuing. Keep every part that the review identifies as correct.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** $f(x)=O(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $|f(x)|\le C|g(x)|$ near $a$ for some constant $C>0$.

**Worked example to compare:** $\sin x=O(x)$ as $x\to0$ because $|\sin x|\le|x|$.

**Boundary to compare:** $f=O(g)$ does not imply $f/g\to1$; boundedness of the ratio is weaker than asymptotic equivalence.

### Week 20 — Permutations · Signature

**Definition.** The signature is the homomorphism from the symmetric group to $\{\pm1\}$ that assigns $-1$ to a transposition.

**Example.** A $k$-cycle has signature $(-1)^{k-1}$.

**Boundary.** The number of transpositions in a decomposition is not unique, but its parity is.

**Proof target.** Prove that a matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

**Decisive proof route.** If $A$ is invertible, $1=\det I=\det(A A^{-1})=det A\det A^{-1}$, so $\det A\ne0$. If $\det A\ne0$, the adjugate identity $A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I$ gives the inverse.

### Week 18 — Linear maps · Matrix

**Definition.** The matrix of a linear map records the coordinates of the images of basis vectors in chosen domain and codomain bases.

**Example.** The columns of the standard matrix of $T(x,y)=(x+y,y)$ are $(1,0)^T$ and $(1,1)^T$.

**Boundary.** A matrix represents a map only after the two bases and their order are fixed.

**Proof target.** Prove that the matrix of the identity map between two bases is invertible.

**Decisive proof route.** The identity map has an inverse—again the identity map—regardless of bases. Matrices turn composition into multiplication, so the two change-of-basis matrices multiply to the identity and are therefore invertible.

### Week 13 — Integer arithmetic · Bézout identity

**Definition.** Bézout's identity states that $\gcd(a,b)$ is an integer combination $ua+vb$.

**Example.** $\gcd(30,18)=6=(-1)30+2\cdot18$.

**Boundary.** The equation $ua+vb=1$ is possible exactly when $a$ and $b$ are coprime.

**Proof target.** Prove Euclid's lemma from Bézout's identity.

**Decisive proof route.** If $p\mid ab$ and $\gcd(p,a)=1$, choose $u,v$ with $up+va=1$. Multiplying by $b$ gives $b=upb+vab$, and both terms are divisible by $p$, so $p\mid b$.

### Week 5 — Real numbers · Supremum

**Definition.** The supremum of a nonempty set bounded above is an upper bound no larger than any other upper bound.

**Example.** For $A=(0,1)$, $\sup A=1$ although $1\notin A$.

**Boundary.** A supremum need not be a maximum and need not belong to the set.

**Proof target.** Prove that if $s=\sup A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, some $a\in A$ satisfies $s-\varepsilon<a\le s$.

**Decisive proof route.** Because $s=\sup A$, $s$ is an upper bound, so every $a\in A$ satisfies $a\le s$. If no $a$ satisfied $a>s-\varepsilon$, then $s-\varepsilon$ would be an upper bound smaller than $s$, contradicting leastness.

## Why this matters

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: An asymptotic expansion lists successive comparison terms with a remainder smaller than the last retained scale. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 21: $f=o(g)$ means $f/g\to0$ where the quotient is defined; $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to1$. Week 6: A sequence $(u_n)$ converges to $\ell$ when every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually satisfies $|u_n-\ell|<\varepsilon$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Asymptotic comparison · Expansion

An asymptotic expansion lists successive comparison terms with a remainder smaller than the last retained scale.

### Complete worked problem

Derive an asymptotic expansion of $1/(1-x)$ through the $x^2$ term as $x\to0$, with a justified remainder.

### Complete worked derivation

The finite geometric identity gives, for $x\ne1$,

$$\frac1{1-x}=1+x+x^2+\frac{x^3}{1-x}.$$

Near $0$, the factor $1/(1-x)$ remains bounded. Therefore

$$\frac{x^3/(1-x)}{x^2}=\frac{x}{1-x}\longrightarrow0.$$

Hence $x^3/(1-x)=o(x^2)$, and the requested expansion is

$$\frac1{1-x}=1+x+x^2+o(x^2)\qquad(x\to0).$$

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Remainders cannot be transformed without checking their scale. In particular, dividing an expansion by a quantity that tends to zero can enlarge the remainder and invalidate the claimed order.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

content.markdown: You are in **MPSI S2**. This page follows the week 22 syllabus requirement: Asymptotic expansions and parameter problems.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can write a complete proof of this exact target: derive the reciprocal expansion by multiplying an unknown quadratic expansion and matching coefficients.

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Derive the reciprocal expansion by multiplying an unknown quadratic expansion and matching coefficients.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: An asymptotic expansion lists successive comparison terms with a remainder smaller than the last retained scale. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 21: $f=o(g)$ means $f/g\to0$ where the quotient is defined; $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to1$. Week 19: An algebraic structure is a set with operations satisfying named axioms. A morphism preserves the relevant operations. Week 14: Elementary row operations preserve the set of solutions of a linear system. Week 6: A sequence $(u_n)$ converges to $\ell$ when every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually satisfies $|u_n-\ell|<\varepsilon$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to derive the reciprocal expansion by multiplying an unknown quadratic expansion and matching coefficients.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

**Definition to compare:** An asymptotic expansion lists successive comparison terms with a remainder smaller than the last retained scale.

**Worked example to compare:** $\log(1+x)=x-x^2/2+o(x^2)$ as $x\to0$.

**Boundary to compare:** Terms cannot be divided or composed without checking that the remainder remains controlled.

### Week 21 — Asymptotic comparison · Big-O notation

**Definition.** $f(x)=O(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $|f(x)|\le C|g(x)|$ near $a$ for some constant $C>0$.

**Example.** $\sin x=O(x)$ as $x\to0$ because $|\sin x|\le|x|$.

**Boundary.** $f=O(g)$ does not imply $f/g\to1$; boundedness of the ratio is weaker than asymptotic equivalence.

**Proof target.** Prove that equivalence is transitive.

**Decisive proof route.** If $a\sim b$ and $b\sim c$, the defining relation property for the present equivalence composes the two witnesses to give $a\sim c$. The proof must name that composition; the word 'equivalent' alone is not a justification.

### Week 19 — Algebra · Morphism

**Definition.** A morphism preserves the operations and distinguished elements of the algebraic structures involved.

**Example.** Evaluation $P\mapsto P(a)$ is a ring morphism from $K[x]$ to $K$.

**Boundary.** A function between groups is not a homomorphism merely because it is bijective.

**Proof target.** Prove that the kernel of a group morphism is a normal subgroup.

**Decisive proof route.** If $x\in\ker\varphi$ and $g$ lies in the group, then $\varphi(gxg^{-1})=\varphi(g)e\varphi(g)^{-1}=e$. Thus the kernel is stable under conjugation and is normal.

### Week 14 — Matrices · Gaussian elimination

**Definition.** Gaussian elimination uses row swaps, nonzero row scaling, and row replacement to reach an equivalent echelon system.

**Example.** Replacing $R_2$ by $R_2-2R_1$ preserves the solution set.

**Boundary.** A row may not be divided by an expression unless it is known to be nonzero.

**Proof target.** Prove that replacing one equation by itself plus a multiple of another preserves the solution set.

**Decisive proof route.** Replacing $E_i$ by $E_i+\lambda E_j$ does not change any common solution because a solution of the old equations satisfies the new one. Conversely, subtracting $\lambda E_j$ recovers $E_i$, so every solution of the new system solves the old one.

### Week 6 — Sequences · Convergence

**Definition.** $(u_n)$ converges to $\ell$ when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some $N$ makes $|u_n-\ell|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$.

**Example.** $u_n=1/n$ tends to $0$: choose $N>1/\varepsilon$.

**Boundary.** Checking many large indices numerically does not prove the quantified tail condition.

**Proof target.** Prove that a real sequence has at most one limit.

**Decisive proof route.** If $u_n\to a$ and $u_n\to b$, choose $N$ so both distances are below $\varepsilon/2$ for $n\ge N$. Then $|a-b|\le|a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $a=b$.

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: The integral of a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is the signed area encoded by the limit of Riemann sums. ## Define the objects in integration on a segment

The integral of a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is the signed area encoded by the limit of Riemann sums.

### A complete first example

$\int_0^1x\,dx=[x^2/2]_0^1=1/2$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

Changing the order of endpoints changes the sign: $\int_b^a f=-\int_a^b f$.

### Exact definition or theorem: Integration · Substitution

Substitution applies the chain rule inside an integral and transforms both the integrand and the bounds.

### Complete worked problem

Evaluate $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\cos x\,dx$ by the substitution $u=\sin x$, including the transformed bounds.

### Complete worked derivation

On $[0,\pi/2]$, set $u=\sin x$. Then $du=\cos x\,dx$. The lower bound $x=0$ becomes $u=0$, and the upper bound $x=\pi/2$ becomes $u=1$. Therefore

$$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\cos x\,dx=\int_0^1u\,du=\left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_0^1=\frac12.$$

Both the differential and the bounds are now expressed in the same variable, so the substitution is complete.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Keeping the old bounds $0$ and $\pi/2$ after changing the integrand to the variable $u$ mixes two coordinate systems. A definite-integral substitution must transform the bounds or explicitly substitute back before evaluation.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can write a complete proof of this exact target: derive integration by parts from the product rule and the fundamental theorem.

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Derive integration by parts from the product rule and the fundamental theorem.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: The fundamental theorem links integration and differentiation: if $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$ for continuous $f$, then $F'=f$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 22: An asymptotic expansion lists successive scales together with a remainder smaller than the final retained scale. Week 20: The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear form on columns that equals $1$ on the standard basis. Week 15: Euclidean division writes $A=BQ+R$ with $\deg R<\deg B$ when $B\ne0$. Week 7: A subsequence has the form $(u_{\varphi(n)})$ where $\varphi$ is strictly increasing. A cluster value is a limit of some convergent subsequence. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to derive integration by parts from the product rule and the fundamental theorem.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

## Use the feedback

Read the earliest important issue first. Rewrite that step before continuing. Keep every part that the review identifies as correct.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** The fundamental theorem links integration and differentiation: if $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$ for continuous $f$, then $F'=f$.

**Worked example to compare:** $d[\int_0^x e^{-t^2}dt]/dx=e^{-x^2}$.

**Boundary to compare:** The integrand's dummy variable and the upper-limit variable play different roles.

### Week 22 — Asymptotic comparison · Expansion

**Definition.** An asymptotic expansion lists successive comparison terms with a remainder smaller than the last retained scale.

**Example.** $\log(1+x)=x-x^2/2+o(x^2)$ as $x\to0$.

**Boundary.** Terms cannot be divided or composed without checking that the remainder remains controlled.

**Proof target.** Derive the reciprocal expansion by multiplying an unknown quadratic expansion and matching coefficients.

**Decisive proof route.** Assume $(1+ax+bx^2)(1+cx+dx^2)=1+O(x^3)$. Matching the $x$ coefficient gives $c=-a$; matching $x^2$ gives $d=a^2-b$. Hence $(1+ax+bx^2)^{-1}=1-ax+(a^2-b)x^2+O(x^3)$.

### Week 20 — Permutations · Signature

**Definition.** The signature is the homomorphism from the symmetric group to $\{\pm1\}$ that assigns $-1$ to a transposition.

**Example.** A $k$-cycle has signature $(-1)^{k-1}$.

**Boundary.** The number of transpositions in a decomposition is not unique, but its parity is.

**Proof target.** Prove that a matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

**Decisive proof route.** If $A$ is invertible, $1=\det I=\det(A A^{-1})=det A\det A^{-1}$, so $\det A\ne0$. If $\det A\ne0$, the adjugate identity $A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I$ gives the inverse.

### Week 15 — Polynomials · Roots

**Definition.** $\alpha$ is a root of $P$ exactly when $P(\alpha)=0$, equivalently when $x-\alpha$ divides $P$.

**Example.** $2$ is a root of $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$.

**Boundary.** A degree-$d$ nonzero polynomial has at most $d$ distinct roots; the zero polynomial is the exceptional case.

**Proof target.** Prove that a polynomial has a repeated root exactly when it shares a nonconstant gcd with its derivative.

**Decisive proof route.** A repeated root $a$ makes both $P(a)$ and $P'(a)$ zero, so $X-a$ divides their gcd. Conversely, if a nonconstant gcd has a root $a$, then $P(a)=P'(a)=0$, and factoring $P=(X-a)Q$ gives $Q(a)=0$, hence $(X-a)^2\mid P$.

### Week 7 — Sequences · Cluster values

**Definition.** A cluster value of a sequence is the limit of at least one convergent subsequence.

**Example.** For $u_n=(-1)^n$, the cluster values are $-1$ and $1$.

**Boundary.** A value approached by finitely many terms only is not a cluster value.

**Proof target.** Prove that every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit.

**Decisive proof route.** Let $u_n\to\ell$ and let $u_{n_k}$ be a subsequence. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ with $n\ge N\Rightarrow|u_n-\ell|<\varepsilon$. Since $n_k\ge k$, every $k\ge N$ also satisfies $|u_{n_k}-\ell|<\varepsilon$.

## Exact task being assessed

**Deliberate review checkpoint.** Without notes, state only the definition of Integration · Fundamental theorem of calculus and one decisive check from its source week. Name one likely error, but leave the full scheduled retrieval and correction for the exit activity.

## Task-specific reference for Integration · Fundamental theorem of calculus

**Definition.** The fundamental theorem links integration and differentiation: if $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$ for continuous $f$, then $F'=f$.

**Valid case.** $d[\int_0^x e^{-t^2}dt]/dx=e^{-x^2}$.

**Boundary.** The integrand's dummy variable and the upper-limit variable play different roles.

**Scheduled review answer key.**

### Week 22 — Asymptotic comparison · Expansion

**Definition.** An asymptotic expansion lists successive comparison terms with a remainder smaller than the last retained scale.

**Example.** $\log(1+x)=x-x^2/2+o(x^2)$ as $x\to0$.

**Boundary.** Terms cannot be divided or composed without checking that the remainder remains controlled.

**Proof target.** Derive the reciprocal expansion by multiplying an unknown quadratic expansion and matching coefficients.

**Decisive proof route.** Assume $(1+ax+bx^2)(1+cx+dx^2)=1+O(x^3)$. Matching the $x$ coefficient gives $c=-a$; matching $x^2$ gives $d=a^2-b$. Hence $(1+ax+bx^2)^{-1}=1-ax+(a^2-b)x^2+O(x^3)$.

### Week 20 — Permutations · Signature

**Definition.** The signature is the homomorphism from the symmetric group to $\{\pm1\}$ that assigns $-1$ to a transposition.

**Example.** A $k$-cycle has signature $(-1)^{k-1}$.

**Boundary.** The number of transpositions in a decomposition is not unique, but its parity is.

**Proof target.** Prove that a matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

**Decisive proof route.** If $A$ is invertible, $1=\det I=\det(A A^{-1})=det A\det A^{-1}$, so $\det A\ne0$. If $\det A\ne0$, the adjugate identity $A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I$ gives the inverse.

### Week 15 — Polynomials · Roots

**Definition.** $\alpha$ is a root of $P$ exactly when $P(\alpha)=0$, equivalently when $x-\alpha$ divides $P$.

**Example.** $2$ is a root of $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$.

**Boundary.** A degree-$d$ nonzero polynomial has at most $d$ distinct roots; the zero polynomial is the exceptional case.

**Proof target.** Prove that a polynomial has a repeated root exactly when it shares a nonconstant gcd with its derivative.

**Decisive proof route.** A repeated root $a$ makes both $P(a)$ and $P'(a)$ zero, so $X-a$ divides their gcd. Conversely, if a nonconstant gcd has a root $a$, then $P(a)=P'(a)=0$, and factoring $P=(X-a)Q$ gives $Q(a)=0$, hence $(X-a)^2\mid P$.

### Week 7 — Sequences · Cluster values

**Definition.** A cluster value of a sequence is the limit of at least one convergent subsequence.

**Example.** For $u_n=(-1)^n$, the cluster values are $-1$ and $1$.

**Boundary.** A value approached by finitely many terms only is not a cluster value.

**Proof target.** Prove that every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit.

**Decisive proof route.** Let $u_n\to\ell$ and let $u_{n_k}$ be a subsequence. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ with $n\ge N\Rightarrow|u_n-\ell|<\varepsilon$. Since $n_k\ge k$, every $k\ge N$ also satisfies $|u_{n_k}-\ell|<\varepsilon$.

## Passing standard for this response

content.markdown: You are in **MPSI S2**. This page follows the week 24 syllabus requirement: Summation by parts and Riemann sums.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can state the defining conditions for Summation · Summation by parts, verify the supplied example, and identify why the boundary case fails.

## Why this matters

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: Summation by parts is the discrete product rule used to transfer a difference from one sequence to another. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 23: The Riemann integral is the limit of weighted sums when the mesh tends to zero; for continuous functions it measures signed area and defines primitives. Week 21: $f=o(g)$ means $f/g\to0$ where the quotient is defined; $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to1$. Week 16: A subset $F$ of a vector space is a subspace when it contains $0$ and is closed under linear combinations. Week 8: A function is continuous at $a$ when $f(x)$ approaches $f(a)$ whenever $x$ approaches $a$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Define the objects in summation by parts and riemann sums

Summation by parts is the discrete product rule used to transfer a difference from one sequence to another.

### A complete first example

$\sum_{k=1}^n a_k(b_{k+1}-b_k)=a_nb_{n+1}-a_1b_1-\sum_{k=2}^n b_k(a_k-a_{k-1})$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

Index endpoints must be derived rather than guessed; one shifted term changes the boundary.

content.title: Week 24, day 2: Follow the method
content.markdown: You are in **MPSI S2**. This page follows the week 24 syllabus requirement: Summation by parts and Riemann sums.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can apply a definition-first method to a complete Riemann sums · Sum verification and check its boundary.

## Why this matters

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A Riemann sum samples a function on a fine partition and converges to its integral under the theorem's hypotheses. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 23: The Riemann integral is the limit of weighted sums when the mesh tends to zero; for continuous functions it measures signed area and defines primitives. Week 21: $f=o(g)$ means $f/g\to0$ where the quotient is defined; $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to1$. Week 16: A subset $F$ of a vector space is a subspace when it contains $0$ and is closed under linear combinations. Week 8: A function is continuous at $a$ when $f(x)$ approaches $f(a)$ whenever $x$ approaches $a$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Riemann sums · Sum

A Riemann sum samples a function on a fine partition and converges to its integral under the theorem's hypotheses.

### Complete worked problem

Compute $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k/n)^3$ by identifying a precise Riemann sum.

### Complete worked derivation

Partition $[0,1]$ into $n$ intervals of width $1/n$ and use the right endpoint $k/n$ in the $k$th interval. The displayed expression is exactly the right-endpoint Riemann sum for the continuous function $f(x)=x^3$. Therefore

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac{k}{n}\right)^3=\int_0^1x^3\,dx=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^1=\frac14.$$

Continuity supplies the convergence theorem, while the factor $1/n$ is the mesh width.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

The sum $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k/n)^3$ without the factor $1/n$ is not the same Riemann sum and grows on the order of $n$. Recognizing sampled values alone is insufficient; the mesh factor is essential.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

content.markdown: You are in **MPSI S2**. This page follows the week 24 syllabus requirement: Summation by parts and Riemann sums.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can write a complete proof of this exact target: derive finite summation by parts by expanding and shifting indices.

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Derive finite summation by parts by expanding and shifting indices.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: Summation by parts is the discrete product rule used to transfer a difference from one sequence to another. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 23: The Riemann integral is the limit of weighted sums when the mesh tends to zero; for continuous functions it measures signed area and defines primitives. Week 21: $f=o(g)$ means $f/g\to0$ where the quotient is defined; $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to1$. Week 16: A subset $F$ of a vector space is a subspace when it contains $0$ and is closed under linear combinations. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to derive finite summation by parts by expanding and shifting indices.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: the kernel of a linear map is a subspace

Let $T:E\to F$ be linear. We prove that $\ker T$ is a vector subspace of $E$.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** Summation by parts is the discrete product rule used to transfer a difference from one sequence to another.

**Worked example to compare:** $\sum_{k=1}^n a_k(b_{k+1}-b_k)=a_nb_{n+1}-a_1b_1-\sum_{k=2}^n b_k(a_k-a_{k-1})$.

**Boundary to compare:** Index endpoints must be derived rather than guessed; one shifted term changes the boundary.

### Week 23 — Integration · Fundamental theorem of calculus

**Definition.** The fundamental theorem links integration and differentiation: if $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)dt$ for continuous $f$, then $F'=f$.

**Example.** $d[\int_0^x e^{-t^2}dt]/dx=e^{-x^2}$.

**Boundary.** The integrand's dummy variable and the upper-limit variable play different roles.

**Proof target.** Derive integration by parts from the product rule and the fundamental theorem.

**Decisive proof route.** Integrate $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$ on $[a,b]$. The fundamental theorem gives $u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)=\int u'v+\int uv'$, and rearrangement yields integration by parts.

### Week 21 — Asymptotic comparison · Big-O notation

**Definition.** $f(x)=O(g(x))$ as $x\to a$ means that $|f(x)|\le C|g(x)|$ near $a$ for some constant $C>0$.

**Example.** $\sin x=O(x)$ as $x\to0$ because $|\sin x|\le|x|$.

**Boundary.** $f=O(g)$ does not imply $f/g\to1$; boundedness of the ratio is weaker than asymptotic equivalence.

**Proof target.** Prove that equivalence is transitive.

**Decisive proof route.** If $a\sim b$ and $b\sim c$, the defining relation property for the present equivalence composes the two witnesses to give $a\sim c$. The proof must name that composition; the word 'equivalent' alone is not a justification.

### Week 16 — Vector spaces · Direct sums

**Definition.** $V=E\oplus F$ means every $v\in V$ has a unique decomposition $v=e+f$ with $e\in E$ and $f\in F$.

**Example.** $\mathbb R^2=\operatorname{span}(e_1)\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_2)$.

**Boundary.** The condition $E+F=V$ is not enough; uniqueness also requires $E\cap F=\{0\}$.

**Proof target.** Prove that $E=F\oplus G$ exactly when every vector has a unique decomposition $f+g$.

**Decisive proof route.** If $E=F\oplus G$, existence comes from $E=F+G$ and uniqueness from $F\cap G=\{0\}$. Conversely, unique decompositions imply every vector lies in $F+G$, and a vector in $F\cap G$ has decompositions $v+0=0+v$, so it must be zero.

### Week 8 — Real functions · Intermediate value theorem

**Definition.** A continuous real function on an interval takes every value between any two of its values.

**Example.** Since $x^3-x-1$ changes sign between $1$ and $2$, it has a root in $(1,2)$.

**Boundary.** The intermediate value theorem gives existence, not uniqueness, and requires continuity on the full interval.

**Proof target.** Prove that a continuous function with opposite signs at the endpoints has a zero between them.

**Decisive proof route.** For continuous $f$ on $[a,b]$ with $f(a)f(b)\le0$, the intermediate value theorem applies because zero lies between the endpoint values. Hence some $c\in[a,b]$ satisfies $f(c)=0$; strict opposite signs place $c$ in $(a,b)$.
