## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Prove an integral-comparison bound for a positive decreasing series.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: The remainder after $n$ terms is the tail $R_n=\sum_{k>n}u_k$, estimated with a theorem suited to the terms. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 45: A vector series converges when its partial sums converge in the normed space. Week 43: Two norms are equivalent when each bounds the other up to positive constants. A compact set is one from which every sequence has a convergent subsequence with limit in the set. Week 38: The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least degree that annihilates the endomorphism. Week 30: A function on $\mathbb R^2$ is differentiable when one linear map approximates all small changes, not only changes along coordinate axes. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove an integral-comparison bound for a positive decreasing series.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 46: A convergence test is chosen from the sign, comparison scale, quotient, root, or oscillation structure of the terms. Week 31: A synthesis week introduces no core concept. It combines established concepts under time and communication constraints. ## Define the objects in pointwise and uniform convergence

$f_n\to f$ pointwise when, for each fixed $x$, the scalar sequence $f_n(x)$ tends to $f(x)$.

### A complete first example

$x^n\to0$ for each $x\in[0,1)$ but equals $1$ at $x=1$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

The index at which accuracy begins may depend on $x$, so pointwise convergence gives no uniform control.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: $f_n\to f$ uniformly when $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 46: A convergence test is chosen from the sign, comparison scale, quotient, root, or oscillation structure of the terms. Week 44: A path from $x$ to $y$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to E$ with endpoints $x,y$. Week 39: The adjoint $u^*$ is defined by $\langle u(x),y\rangle=\langle x,u^*(y)\rangle$ for all $x,y$. ## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Sequences of functions · Uniform

$f_n\to f$ uniformly when $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$.

### Complete worked problem

Prove that $f_n(x)=x^2/n$ converges uniformly to $0$ on $[-2,2]$ by computing the exact supremum error.

### Complete worked derivation

For every $x\in[-2,2]$, one has $|x|^2\le4$. Therefore

$$\sup_{x\in[-2,2]}|f_n(x)-0|=\sup_{x\in[-2,2]}\frac{x^2}{n}=\frac4n.$$

The supremum is attained at $x=\pm2$, and $4/n\to0$. This is exactly the supremum criterion for uniform convergence, so $f_n\to0$ uniformly on the whole interval.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Pointwise convergence does not imply uniform convergence. On $[0,1]$, $x^n$ tends pointwise to a discontinuous limit that equals $0$ on $[0,1)$ and $1$ at $1$, so the convergence cannot be uniform.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** $f_n\to f$ uniformly when $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$.

**Worked example to compare:** $x/n\to0$ uniformly on $[0,1]$ because the supremum error is $1/n$.

**Boundary to compare:** Pointwise convergence to a discontinuous limit on a compact interval cannot be uniform when all $f_n$ are continuous.

### Week 46 — Numerical series · Remainder

**Definition.** The remainder after $n$ terms is the tail $R_n=\sum_{k>n}u_k$, estimated with a theorem suited to the terms.

**Example.** For a positive decreasing function, integral comparison bounds the series tail by neighboring improper integrals.

**Boundary.** A remainder estimate must control the full infinite tail, not only the next term unless an alternating-series theorem applies.

**Proof target.** Prove an integral-comparison bound for a positive decreasing series.

**Decisive proof route.** For positive decreasing $f$ with $u_n=f(n)$, compare each rectangle with the integrals on $[n,n+1]$. Summing gives the two-sided bounds between the series tail and adjacent improper-integral tails.

### Week 44 — Topology · Path-connected sets

**Definition.** A set is path connected when any two points can be joined by a continuous path lying in the set.

**Example.** Every convex subset of a normed space is path connected by the line segment path.

**Boundary.** Connectedness need not imply path connectedness in general topological spaces.

**Proof target.** Prove that the continuous image of a path-connected set is path connected.

**Decisive proof route.** For any two points $f(x),f(y)$ in the image, choose a path $\gamma$ in the original set from $x$ to $y$. The composition $f\circ\gamma$ is continuous and joins $f(x)$ to $f(y)$.

### Week 39 — Euclidean spaces · Isometry

**Definition.** A linear isometry preserves norms, equivalently inner products in a real Euclidean space.

**Example.** Reflections and rotations are linear isometries.

**Boundary.** A general affine isometry may include a translation and therefore need not be linear.

**Proof target.** Prove that a linear map is an isometry exactly when $u^*u=I$.

**Decisive proof route.** The norm identity $\|ux\|^2=\langle u^*ux,x\rangle$ shows that $u^*u=I$ implies isometry. Conversely, preserving norms and polarizing gives $\langle ux,uy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$, hence $u^*u=I$.

### Week 31 — Determinants · Multilinear

**Definition.** The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear function of the columns that equals $1$ on the standard basis.

**Example.** Adding a multiple of one column to another leaves the determinant unchanged.

**Boundary.** Linearity holds in one column at a time, not under simultaneous arbitrary changes to several columns.

**Proof target.** Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$. Audit the false claim “every entry of $A$ is nonzero, so $A$ is invertible.” Compute the determinant, identify the earliest unsupported implication, and rewrite the argument using the correct invertibility criterion.

**Decisive proof route.** For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, the characteristic polynomial is $(X-1)^2$ but the eigenspace is one-dimensional; equivalently, the minimal polynomial is $(X-1)^2$. Splitting alone is insufficient, so $A$ is not diagonalizable.

### Week 46 — Numerical series · Remainder

**Definition.** The remainder after $n$ terms is the tail $R_n=\sum_{k>n}u_k$, estimated with a theorem suited to the terms.

**Example.** For a positive decreasing function, integral comparison bounds the series tail by neighboring improper integrals.

**Proof target.** Prove an integral-comparison bound for a positive decreasing series.

### Week 44 — Topology · Path-connected sets

**Definition.** A set is path connected when any two points can be joined by a continuous path lying in the set.

**Example.** Every convex subset of a normed space is path connected by the line segment path.

**Boundary.** Connectedness need not imply path connectedness in general topological spaces.

**Proof target.** Prove that the continuous image of a path-connected set is path connected.

**Decisive proof route.** For any two points $f(x),f(y)$ in the image, choose a path $\gamma$ in the original set from $x$ to $y$. The composition $f\circ\gamma$ is continuous and joins $f(x)$ to $f(y)$.

**Definition.** A linear isometry preserves norms, equivalently inner products in a real Euclidean space.

**Example.** Reflections and rotations are linear isometries.

**Boundary.** A general affine isometry may include a translation and therefore need not be linear.

**Proof target.** Prove that a linear map is an isometry exactly when $u^*u=I$.

**Decisive proof route.** The norm identity $\|ux\|^2=\langle u^*ux,x\rangle$ shows that $u^*u=I$ implies isometry. Conversely, preserving norms and polarizing gives $\langle ux,uy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$, hence $u^*u=I$.

### Week 31 — Determinants · Multilinear

**Definition.** The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear function of the columns that equals $1$ on the standard basis.

**Example.** Adding a multiple of one column to another leaves the determinant unchanged.

**Boundary.** Linearity holds in one column at a time, not under simultaneous arbitrary changes to several columns.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can apply a definition-first method to a complete Series of functions · Integrate verification and check its boundary.

## Why this matters

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: Uniform convergence of continuous terms on a compact interval permits termwise integration. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 47: Uniform convergence means one index works for every point: $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$. Week 45: A vector series converges when its partial sums converge in the normed space. Week 40: A self-adjoint map satisfies $u=u^*$. ## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Series of functions · Integrate

Uniform convergence of continuous terms on a compact interval permits termwise integration.

### Complete worked problem

On $[0,1]$, justify termwise integration of $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(x/2)^k$ and compute the integral of its sum.

### Complete worked derivation

For $x\in[0,1]$, $|(x/2)^k|\le2^{-k}$, and $\sum2^{-k}$ converges. The Weierstrass test gives uniform convergence of the continuous terms. Termwise integration is therefore valid:

$$\int_0^1\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^kdx=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^k(k+1)}.$$

The geometric sum is $1/(1-x/2)$, so the same integral equals

$$\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1-x/2}=2\log2.$$

Thus the series of integrals converges to $2\log2$.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Pointwise convergence by itself does not justify exchanging an infinite sum and an integral. A uniform-convergence theorem or another suitable integration theorem must be checked first.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

## Today's learning goal

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Prove the Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: $\sum f_n$ converges normally when $\sum\|f_n\|_\infty$ converges. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 47: Uniform convergence means one index works for every point: $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$. Week 45: A vector series converges when its partial sums converge in the normed space. Week 40: A self-adjoint map satisfies $u=u^*$. In finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces it has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Week 32: A mixed paper tests concept selection as well as execution: the first task is to name the chapter, theorem, and hypotheses before calculating. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove the Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

## Use the feedback

Read the earliest important issue first. Rewrite that step before continuing. Keep every part that the review identifies as correct.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** The Weierstrass approximation theorem says every continuous real function on a compact interval is uniformly approximable by polynomials.

**Worked example to compare:** Bernstein polynomials approximate a continuous function uniformly on $[0,1]$.

**Boundary to compare:** The theorem gives uniform approximation, not equality with one finite polynomial.

### Week 47 — Sequences of functions · Uniform

**Definition.** $f_n\to f$ uniformly when $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$.

**Example.** $x/n\to0$ uniformly on $[0,1]$ because the supremum error is $1/n$.

**Boundary.** Pointwise convergence to a discontinuous limit on a compact interval cannot be uniform when all $f_n$ are continuous.

**Proof target.** Prove that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

**Decisive proof route.** Given $f_n\to f$ uniformly and $x\to a$, choose $n$ so $\|f-f_n\|_\infty<\varepsilon/3$, then use continuity of $f_n$ at $a$. The triangle inequality splits $|f(x)-f(a)|$ into three terms below $\varepsilon/3$.

### Week 45 — Numerical series · Vector

**Definition.** A vector series converges when its partial sums converge in the vector-space norm.

**Example.** In finite dimension, $\sum v_n$ converges exactly when every coordinate series converges.

**Boundary.** Coordinatewise reasoning requires a fixed finite-dimensional basis or a theorem appropriate to the space.

**Proof target.** Prove that convergence of every coordinate series implies convergence of the vector series in finite dimension.

**Decisive proof route.** In a finite basis, coordinatewise convergence gives a candidate vector whose coordinates are the coordinate sums. Norm equivalence bounds the vector tail by a constant times the maximum or sum of coordinate tails, so the vector partial sums converge.

### Week 40 — Euclidean spaces · Self-adjoint operators

**Definition.** An endomorphism $T$ of a Euclidean space is self-adjoint when $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all vectors $x,y$, equivalently $T=T^*$.

**Example.** A real symmetric matrix represents a self-adjoint endomorphism in an orthonormal basis.

**Boundary.** A matrix that is symmetric in a nonorthonormal basis need not represent a self-adjoint map.

**Proof target.** Prove that eigenvectors of a self-adjoint map with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

**Decisive proof route.** For $Tu=\lambda u$, $Tv=\mu v$, and $T=T^*$, $\lambda\langle u,v\rangle=\langle Tu,v\rangle=\langle u,Tv\rangle=\mu\langle u,v\rangle$. Distinct eigenvalues force $\langle u,v\rangle=0$.

### Week 32 — Real functions · Intermediate value theorem

**Definition.** A continuous real function on an interval takes every value between any two of its values.

**Example.** Since $x^3-x-1$ changes sign between $1$ and $2$, it has a root in $(1,2)$.

**Boundary.** The intermediate value theorem gives existence, not uniqueness, and requires continuity on the full interval.

**Proof target.** Audit the false proof “$f(x)=x^3-x$ changes sign somewhere, so it has a zero in $(0,1)$.” State the exact endpoint data and continuity hypothesis needed for the intermediate value theorem, then write a correct existence statement.

**Decisive proof route.** The statement '$x^3-x$ has a zero in $(0,1)$ because it changes sign' is invalid: both endpoint values are zero and no strict sign change was shown. A correct IVT claim uses a specified interval and verified endpoint values of opposite sign, or concludes only the endpoint zeros here.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Power series · Domain

The convergence domain is the open disc together with whichever boundary points converge after separate analysis.

### Complete worked problem

Determine the full complex convergence domain of the power series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}z^n/n^2$.

### Complete worked derivation

The root test gives

$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sqrt[n]{1/n^2}=1,$$

so the radius of convergence is $R=1$. The series converges absolutely for $|z|<1$ and diverges for $|z|>1$ because its terms do not tend to zero. On the boundary $|z|=1$,

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left|\frac{z^n}{n^2}\right|=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2}<\infty.$$

Thus every boundary point converges absolutely, and the full domain is the closed unit disc $\{z:|z|\le1\}$.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

The radius alone does not decide boundary points. For $\sum z^n/n$, the points $z=1$ and $z=-1$ have the same modulus, but the first series diverges and the second converges.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Prove that convergence at one nonzero point implies absolute convergence at every point of smaller modulus.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A power series has a radius $R$ with absolute convergence for $|z|<R$ and divergence for $|z|>R$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 48: Normal convergence means the sup norms of the terms form a convergent numerical series; it implies uniform convergence. Week 46: A convergence test is chosen from the sign, comparison scale, quotient, root, or oscillation structure of the terms. Week 41: A norm is positive, homogeneous, and subadditive. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove that convergence at one nonzero point implies absolute convergence at every point of smaller modulus.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** A power series has a radius $R$ with absolute convergence for $|z|<R$ and divergence for $|z|>R$.

**Worked example to compare:** The geometric power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n$ has radius of convergence $1$.

**Boundary to compare:** The radius criterion gives no automatic answer on the boundary $|z|=R$.

### Week 48 — Series of functions · Normal

**Definition.** $\sum f_n$ converges normally when $\sum\|f_n\|_\infty$ converges.

**Example.** If $|f_n(x)|\le2^{-n}$ for every $x$, the series converges normally.

**Boundary.** Uniform convergence of the series does not by itself imply convergence of the sup-norm series.

**Proof target.** Prove the Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence.

**Decisive proof route.** If $|f_n(x)|\le M_n$ for all $x$ and $\sum M_n$ converges, every uniform tail is bounded by $\sum_{n>N}M_n$, which tends to zero independently of $x$. The uniform Cauchy criterion gives uniform convergence.

### Week 46 — Numerical series · Remainder

**Definition.** The remainder after $n$ terms is the tail $R_n=\sum_{k>n}u_k$, estimated with a theorem suited to the terms.

**Example.** For a positive decreasing function, integral comparison bounds the series tail by neighboring improper integrals.

**Boundary.** A remainder estimate must control the full infinite tail, not only the next term unless an alternating-series theorem applies.

**Proof target.** Prove an integral-comparison bound for a positive decreasing series.

**Decisive proof route.** For positive decreasing $f$ with $u_n=f(n)$, compare each rectangle with the integrals on $[n,n+1]$. Summing gives the two-sided bounds between the series tail and adjacent improper-integral tails.

### Week 41 — Normed vector spaces · Operator

**Definition.** The operator norm is $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|=1}\|Tx\|$ and is the smallest constant with $\|Tx\|\le\|T\|\|x\|$.

**Example.** For a diagonal map in Euclidean norm, the operator norm is the largest absolute diagonal entry.

**Boundary.** The operator norm is not generally the sum of absolute matrix entries.

**Proof target.** Prove that the operator norm is submultiplicative.

**Decisive proof route.** For every $x$, $\|ABx\|\le\|A\|\,\|Bx\|\le\|A\|\,\|B\|\,\|x\|$. Taking the supremum over unit vectors gives $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$.

### Week 33 — Linear maps · Kernel

**Definition.** $\ker T=\{v:T(v)=0\}$ is the subspace of inputs annihilated by a linear map.

**Example.** For $T(x,y)=x+y$, the kernel is $\operatorname{span}(1,-1)$.

**Boundary.** The kernel lives in the domain, not the codomain.

**Proof target.** Rewrite a complete proof that the kernel of a linear map is a subspace. Annotate the job of each paragraph: setup, zero vector, closure under linear combinations, and conclusion.

**Decisive proof route.** For linear $T:E\to F$, state the ambient spaces, show $0\in\ker T$, and prove closure under $\alpha x+\beta y$ using linearity. The four paragraphs respectively establish setup, nonemptiness, closure, and the subspace conclusion.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can state the defining conditions for Power series · Operations, verify the supplied example, and identify why the boundary case fails.

## Why this matters

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: Inside the common convergence disc, power series may be added, scaled, and composed when the inner series stays in the outer domain. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 49: A power series $\sum a_nz^n$ has a radius $R$ such that it converges absolutely for $|z|<R$ and diverges for $|z|>R$. Week 47: Uniform convergence means one index works for every point: $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$. Week 42: A set is open when every point contains a small open ball inside the set; it is closed when it contains the limit of every convergent sequence from the set. Week 34: An ideal is an additive subgroup stable under multiplication by arbitrary ring elements. A quotient ring identifies elements whose difference lies in the ideal. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Define the objects in operations and standard power-series expansions

Inside the common convergence disc, power series may be added, scaled, and composed when the inner series stays in the outer domain.

### A complete first example

Adding $\sum a_nz^n$ and $\sum b_nz^n$ gives coefficients $a_n+b_n$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

Formal composition is not justified when the substituted values leave the convergence disc.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Power series · Cauchy

The product of two power series has Cauchy-product coefficients $c_n=\sum_{k=0}^na_kb_{n-k}$ inside the common disc.

### Complete worked problem

Find the Cauchy-product coefficients of $(\sum_{n\ge0}z^n)(\sum_{n\ge0}2^{-n}z^n)$ and state a disc where the product identity is justified.

### Complete worked derivation

The two series have radii $1$ and $2$, so both converge absolutely for $|z|<1$. The Cauchy coefficient of $z^n$ is

$$c_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}1\cdot2^{-(n-k)}=\sum_{j=0}^{n}2^{-j}=2-2^{-n}.$$

Therefore, on the common disc $|z|<1$,

$$\left(\sum_{n\ge0}z^n\right)\left(\sum_{n\ge0}2^{-n}z^n\right)=\sum_{n\ge0}(2-2^{-n})z^n.$$

The closed forms $1/(1-z)$ and $1/(1-z/2)$ give the same product and check the coefficients.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Formal convolution does not enlarge the justified convergence domain. The product identity above is established inside the common disc; behavior on or beyond its boundary requires a separate argument.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

## Today's learning goal

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Derive one standard expansion from the geometric series and verify the constant of integration.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A power series may be integrated term by term inside its radius, with an independently determined constant. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 49: A power series $\sum a_nz^n$ has a radius $R$ such that it converges absolutely for $|z|<R$ and diverges for $|z|>R$. Week 47: Uniform convergence means one index works for every point: $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$. Week 42: A set is open when every point contains a small open ball inside the set; it is closed when it contains the limit of every convergent sequence from the set. Week 34: An ideal is an additive subgroup stable under multiplication by arbitrary ring elements. A quotient ring identifies elements whose difference lies in the ideal. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to derive one standard expansion from the geometric series and verify the constant of integration.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** A power series may be integrated term by term inside its radius, with an independently determined constant.

**Worked example to compare:** $-\log(1-z)=\sum_{n\ge1}z^n/n$ for $|z|<1$.

**Boundary to compare:** Forgetting the integration constant prevents identification of the correct function.

### Week 49 — Power series · Radius

**Definition.** A power series has a radius $R$ with absolute convergence for $|z|<R$ and divergence for $|z|>R$.

**Example.** The geometric power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n$ has radius of convergence $1$.

**Boundary.** The radius criterion gives no automatic answer on the boundary $|z|=R$.

**Proof target.** Prove that convergence at one nonzero point implies absolute convergence at every point of smaller modulus.

## Today's learning goal

## Why this matters

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A vector-valued derivative is the vector limit of the difference quotient, equivalent to coordinate differentiation in finite dimension. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 50: Inside its open disc of convergence, a power series may be differentiated and integrated term by term without changing the radius. Week 48: Normal convergence means the sup norms of the terms form a convergent numerical series; it implies uniform convergence. Week 43: Two norms are equivalent when each bounds the other up to positive constants. A compact set is one from which every sequence has a convergent subsequence with limit in the set. Week 35: A nonzero vector $v$ is an eigenvector of $u$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ when $u(v)=\lambda v$. Its eigenspace is $\ker(u-\lambda I)$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Define the objects in vector-valued differentiation and integration

A vector-valued derivative is the vector limit of the difference quotient, equivalent to coordinate differentiation in finite dimension.

### A complete first example

For $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, $r'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t)$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

Differentiating coordinates presupposes a finite-dimensional coordinate representation.

## What you need first

Week 48: Normal convergence means the sup norms of the terms form a convergent numerical series; it implies uniform convergence. ## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

### Exact definition or theorem: Vector-valued functions · Integral

A continuous vector-valued function is integrated coordinatewise in finite dimension, producing a basis-independent vector.

### Complete worked problem

Compute the vector integral $\int_0^{\pi}(\cos t,\sin t)\,dt$ in $\mathbb R^2$ and explain the coordinatewise integration step.

### Complete worked derivation

In finite dimension, a continuous vector-valued function is integrated coordinatewise. Hence

$$\int_0^{\pi}(\cos t,\sin t)\,dt=\left(\int_0^{\pi}\cos t\,dt,\int_0^{\pi}\sin t\,dt\right).$$

The first coordinate is $[\sin t]_0^{\pi}=0$, and the second is $[-\cos t]_0^{\pi}=2$. Therefore the vector integral is $(0,2)$. The answer is a vector in the same space as the integrand values.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Integrating the norm gives $\int_0^{\pi}1\,dt=\pi$, whereas the norm of the vector integral is $2$. These quantities satisfy an inequality but are not generally equal.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** Taylor's formula for a vector-valued function applies componentwise with a vector remainder estimate.

**Worked example to compare:** $r(t+h)=r(t)+hr'(t)+O(h^2)$ for a twice differentiable plane curve.

**Boundary to compare:** A componentwise expansion needs one remainder control valid for the chosen vector norm.

### Week 50 — Power series · Integrate

**Definition.** A power series may be integrated term by term inside its radius, with an independently determined constant.

**Example.** $-\log(1-z)=\sum_{n\ge1}z^n/n$ for $|z|<1$.

**Boundary.** Forgetting the integration constant prevents identification of the correct function.

**Proof target.** Derive one standard expansion from the geometric series and verify the constant of integration.

**Decisive proof route.** Start with $1/(1-x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n$ for $|x|<1$. Integrating from zero gives $-\log(1-x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^{n+1}/(n+1)$; the value at zero fixes the integration constant.

### Week 48 — Series of functions · Normal

**Definition.** $\sum f_n$ converges normally when $\sum\|f_n\|_\infty$ converges.

**Example.** If $|f_n(x)|\le2^{-n}$ for every $x$, the series converges normally.

**Boundary.** Uniform convergence of the series does not by itself imply convergence of the sup-norm series.

**Proof target.** Prove the Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence.

**Decisive proof route.** If $|f_n(x)|\le M_n$ for all $x$ and $\sum M_n$ converges, every uniform tail is bounded by $\sum_{n>N}M_n$, which tends to zero independently of $x$. The uniform Cauchy criterion gives uniform convergence.

### Week 43 — Topology · Compactness

**Definition.** A subset of a metric space is compact when every sequence has a convergent subsequence whose limit remains in the set.

**Example.** In $\mathbb R^n$, closed and bounded sets are compact.

**Boundary.** Closed and bounded need not imply compactness in an arbitrary infinite-dimensional normed space.

**Proof target.** Prove that a continuous function on a compact set is bounded.

**Decisive proof route.** If a continuous $f$ on compact $K$ were unbounded, choose $x_n$ with $|f(x_n)|\ge n$. A convergent subsequence $x_{n_k}\to x\in K$ would give bounded $f(x_{n_k})\to f(x)$, a contradiction.

### Week 35 — Linear maps · Eigen

**Definition.** $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ when some nonzero $v$ satisfies $T(v)=\lambda v$.

**Example.** For $\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$, the coordinate axes are eigenspaces for $2$ and $3$.

**Boundary.** The zero vector is never an eigenvector.

**Proof target.** Prove that eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues form a direct sum.

**Decisive proof route.** If $v_i$ are eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues and $\sum v_i=0$, apply a polynomial in $T$ that is one on one eigenvalue and zero on the others. This isolates each $v_i$, so every $v_i=0$ and the eigenspaces form a direct sum.

- **Week 43 — Topology · Compactness:** state the definition, reconstruct a proof of “Prove that a continuous function on a compact set is bounded.”, and name one hypothesis or boundary that would invalidate the argument.
- **Week 35 — Linear maps · Eigen:** state the definition, reconstruct a proof of “Prove that eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues form a direct sum.”, and name one hypothesis or boundary that would invalidate the argument. Classify one likely error and repair the earliest invalid step.

## Task-specific reference for Vector-valued functions · Taylor

**Definition.** Taylor's formula for a vector-valued function applies componentwise with a vector remainder estimate.

**Valid case.** $r(t+h)=r(t)+hr'(t)+O(h^2)$ for a twice differentiable plane curve.

**Boundary.** A componentwise expansion needs one remainder control valid for the chosen vector norm.

**Scheduled review answer key.**

### Week 50 — Power series · Integrate

**Definition.** A power series may be integrated term by term inside its radius, with an independently determined constant.

**Example.** $-\log(1-z)=\sum_{n\ge1}z^n/n$ for $|z|<1$.

**Boundary.** Forgetting the integration constant prevents identification of the correct function.

**Proof target.** Derive one standard expansion from the geometric series and verify the constant of integration.

**Decisive proof route.** Start with $1/(1-x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n$ for $|x|<1$. Integrating from zero gives $-\log(1-x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^{n+1}/(n+1)$; the value at zero fixes the integration constant.

### Week 48 — Series of functions · Normal

**Definition.** $\sum f_n$ converges normally when $\sum\|f_n\|_\infty$ converges.

**Example.** If $|f_n(x)|\le2^{-n}$ for every $x$, the series converges normally.

**Boundary.** Uniform convergence of the series does not by itself imply convergence of the sup-norm series.

**Proof target.** Prove the Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence.

**Decisive proof route.** If $|f_n(x)|\le M_n$ for all $x$ and $\sum M_n$ converges, every uniform tail is bounded by $\sum_{n>N}M_n$, which tends to zero independently of $x$. The uniform Cauchy criterion gives uniform convergence.

### Week 43 — Topology · Compactness

**Definition.** A subset of a metric space is compact when every sequence has a convergent subsequence whose limit remains in the set.

**Example.** In $\mathbb R^n$, closed and bounded sets are compact.

**Boundary.** Closed and bounded need not imply compactness in an arbitrary infinite-dimensional normed space.

**Proof target.** Prove that a continuous function on a compact set is bounded.

**Decisive proof route.** If a continuous $f$ on compact $K$ were unbounded, choose $x_n$ with $|f(x_n)|\ge n$. A convergent subsequence $x_{n_k}\to x\in K$ would give bounded $f(x_{n_k})\to f(x)$, a contradiction.

### Week 35 — Linear maps · Eigen

**Definition.** $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ when some nonzero $v$ satisfies $T(v)=\lambda v$.

**Example.** For $\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$, the coordinate axes are eigenspaces for $2$ and $3$.

**Boundary.** The zero vector is never an eigenvector.

**Proof target.** Prove that eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues form a direct sum.

**Decisive proof route.** If $v_i$ are eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues and $\sum v_i=0$, apply a polynomial in $T$ that is one on one eigenvalue and zero on the others. This isolates each $v_i$, so every $v_i=0$ and the eigenspaces form a direct sum.

The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 51: A vector-valued function is differentiated by a vector limit; in finite dimension this is equivalent to differentiating coordinates. Week 49: A power series $\sum a_nz^n$ has a radius $R$ such that it converges absolutely for $|z|<R$ and diverges for $|z|>R$. ## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Improper integrals · Comparison

Comparison transfers convergence between nonnegative functions with a proven local inequality near the improper endpoint.

### Complete worked problem

Prove by comparison that $\int_1^{\infty}1/(x^2+1)\,dx$ converges, stating which improper endpoint the comparison controls.

### Complete worked derivation

For every $x\ge1$, both functions are nonnegative and

$$0\le\frac1{x^2+1}\le\frac1{x^2}.$$

The comparison is valid near the improper endpoint $+\infty$. Since

$$\int_1^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^2}=1$$

converges, the comparison theorem implies that $\int_1^{\infty}1/(x^2+1)\,dx$ converges. The continuous integrand has no singularity at the finite lower endpoint, so no second improper issue remains.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

An inequality checked only on a bounded interval away from the improper endpoint does not control convergence. The comparison must hold on a full tail $[M,\infty)$, or on a punctured neighborhood of a finite singular endpoint.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

## Today's learning goal

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Prove the $p$-integral convergence criterion by evaluating finite truncations.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: Integration by parts for an improper integral is performed on finite truncations before passing to the limit. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 51: A vector-valued function is differentiated by a vector limit; in finite dimension this is equivalent to differentiating coordinates. Week 49: A power series $\sum a_nz^n$ has a radius $R$ such that it converges absolutely for $|z|<R$ and diverges for $|z|>R$. Week 44: A path from $x$ to $y$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to E$ with endpoints $x,y$. Week 36: An endomorphism is diagonalizable when the space has a basis of eigenvectors. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove the $p$-integral convergence criterion by evaluating finite truncations.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** Integration by parts for an improper integral is performed on finite truncations before passing to the limit.

**Worked example to compare:** $\int_1^R(\log x)/x^2dx$ is integrated by parts first, then $R\to\infty$.

**Boundary to compare:** The limiting boundary term must exist; formal endpoint notation cannot replace that check.

### Week 51 — Vector-valued functions · Taylor

**Definition.** Taylor's formula for a vector-valued function applies componentwise with a vector remainder estimate.

**Example.** $r(t+h)=r(t)+hr'(t)+O(h^2)$ for a twice differentiable plane curve.

**Boundary.** A componentwise expansion needs one remainder control valid for the chosen vector norm.

**Proof target.** Prove that the derivative of a constant-norm curve is orthogonal to the position vector.

**Decisive proof route.** Differentiate $\langle\gamma(t),\gamma(t)\rangle=c^2$. The product rule gives $2\langle\gamma'(t),\gamma(t)\rangle=0$, so velocity is orthogonal to position.

### Week 49 — Power series · Radius

**Definition.** A power series has a radius $R$ with absolute convergence for $|z|<R$ and divergence for $|z|>R$.

**Example.** The geometric power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n$ has radius of convergence $1$.

**Boundary.** The radius criterion gives no automatic answer on the boundary $|z|=R$.

**Proof target.** Prove that convergence at one nonzero point implies absolute convergence at every point of smaller modulus.

**Decisive proof route.** If $\sum a_n z_0^n$ converges for $z_0\ne0$, its terms are bounded: $|a_nz_0^n|\le M$. For $|z|<|z_0|$, $|a_nz^n|\le M(|z|/|z_0|)^n$, and the geometric comparison gives absolute convergence.

### Week 44 — Topology · Path-connected sets

**Definition.** A set is path connected when any two points can be joined by a continuous path lying in the set.

**Example.** Every convex subset of a normed space is path connected by the line segment path.

**Boundary.** Connectedness need not imply path connectedness in general topological spaces.

**Proof target.** Prove that the continuous image of a path-connected set is path connected.

**Decisive proof route.** For any two points $f(x),f(y)$ in the image, choose a path $\gamma$ in the original set from $x$ to $y$. The composition $f\circ\gamma$ is continuous and joins $f(x)$ to $f(y)$.

### Week 36 — Linear maps · Diagonalization

**Definition.** An endomorphism is diagonalizable when the space has a basis of eigenvectors.

**Example.** A real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable.

**Boundary.** Having a characteristic polynomial that splits is not enough when eigenspace dimensions are too small.

**Proof target.** Prove that an endomorphism with a basis of eigenvectors has a diagonal matrix in that basis.

**Decisive proof route.** If $(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ is a basis of eigenvectors with $T(v_i)=\lambda_i v_i$, the $i$th matrix column has only $\lambda_i$ in row $i$. Hence the matrix is diagonal.

## Why this matters

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: Dominated convergence combines pointwise convergence with one integrable majorant independent of the sequence index. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 52: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals near an infinite endpoint or singularity. Dominated convergence combines pointwise convergence with one integrable majorant independent of the sequence index.

### A complete first example

If $|f_n|\le g\in L^1$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise, then $\int f_n\to\int f$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

A different majorant $g_n$ for each $n$ does not satisfy the theorem.

## What you need first

The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 52: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals near an infinite endpoint or singularity. Week 50: Inside its open disc of convergence, a power series may be differentiated and integrated term by term without changing the radius. Week 45: A vector series converges when its partial sums converge in the normed space. Week 37: An endomorphism is triangularizable when some basis gives an upper triangular matrix. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Parameter-dependent integrals · Differentiate

Differentiation under the integral requires a parameter derivative and an integrable bound for that derivative on a neighborhood.

### Complete worked problem

For $F(x)=\int_0^1e^{-xt^2}\,dt$, justify differentiation under the integral for $x\in(-1,1)$ and find $F'(x)$.

### Complete worked derivation

The parameter derivative exists and is

$$\partial_x e^{-xt^2}=-t^2e^{-xt^2}.$$

For $x\in(-1,1)$ and $t\in[0,1]$,

$$|t^2e^{-xt^2}|\le e\,t^2,$$

and $t\mapsto e t^2$ is integrable on $[0,1]$. This single bound works on the whole parameter interval under consideration. The differentiation theorem therefore gives

$$F'(x)=-\int_0^1t^2e^{-xt^2}\,dt.$$

The bound is the step that turns formal differentiation into a justified exchange.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Computing the pointwise derivative of the integrand is not enough. Without an integrable bound that is uniform for nearby parameter values, the derivative and integral cannot be interchanged by this theorem.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 52: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals near an infinite endpoint or singularity. ## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove continuity of a parameter integral using a stated domination theorem.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: a sequence cannot have two limits

Assume that $(u_n)$ converges to both $a$ and $b$. We prove that $a=b$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $u_n\to a$, there is $N_1$ such that $n\ge N_1$ implies $|u_n-a|<\varepsilon/2$. Because $u_n\to b$, there is $N_2$ such that $n\ge N_2$ implies $|u_n-b|<\varepsilon/2$.

Choose $n\ge\max(N_1,N_2)$. The triangle inequality gives

$$|a-b|\le |a-u_n|+|u_n-b|<\varepsilon.$$

This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $|a-b|=0$ and therefore $a=b$.

**Why the paragraphs are in this order.** The first names the assumptions and target. The second expands both convergence assumptions with the same tolerance. The third makes both estimates true at once. The last converts an arbitrarily small distance into equality.

**Example.** $\int_1^R(\log x)/x^2dx$ is integrated by parts first, then $R\to\infty$.

**Decisive proof route.** For $p\ne1$, $\int_1^R x^{-p}dx=(R^{1-p}-1)/(1-p)$, whose limit is finite exactly when $p>1$. For $p=1$, the truncation is $\log R\to\infty$.

**Definition.** A power series may be integrated term by term inside its radius, with an independently determined constant.

**Example.** $-\log(1-z)=\sum_{n\ge1}z^n/n$ for $|z|<1$.

**Boundary.** Forgetting the integration constant prevents identification of the correct function.

**Example.** In finite dimension, $\sum v_n$ converges exactly when every coordinate series converges.

**Boundary.** Coordinatewise reasoning requires a fixed finite-dimensional basis or a theorem appropriate to the space.

**Proof target.** Prove that convergence of every coordinate series implies convergence of the vector series in finite dimension.

**Decisive proof route.** In a finite basis, coordinatewise convergence gives a candidate vector whose coordinates are the coordinate sums. Norm equivalence bounds the vector tail by a constant times the maximum or sum of coordinate tails, so the vector partial sums converge.

**Example.** A strictly upper-triangular $n\times n$ matrix satisfies $N^n=0$.

**Proof target.** Prove that a nilpotent endomorphism has trace zero and determinant zero in positive dimension.

content.markdown: You are in **MP**. This page follows the week 54 syllabus requirement: Countable probability and standard discrete laws.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can state the defining conditions for Probability · Bernoulli, verify the supplied example, and identify why the boundary case fails.

## Why this matters

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A Bernoulli variable takes values $1$ and $0$ with probabilities $p$ and $1-p$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 53: Dominated convergence combines pointwise convergence with one integrable dominating function independent of the sequence index. Week 51: A vector-valued function is differentiated by a vector limit; in finite dimension this is equivalent to differentiating coordinates. Week 46: A convergence test is chosen from the sign, comparison scale, quotient, root, or oscillation structure of the terms. Week 38: The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least degree that annihilates the endomorphism. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Define the objects in countable probability and standard discrete laws

A Bernoulli variable takes values $1$ and $0$ with probabilities $p$ and $1-p$.

### A complete first example

For $X\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$, $E[X]=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

A Bernoulli model describes one binary trial, not a count over several trials.

content.title: Week 54, day 2: Follow the method
content.markdown: You are in **MP**. This page follows the week 54 syllabus requirement: Countable probability and standard discrete laws.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can apply a definition-first method to a complete Probability · Binomial theorem verification and check its boundary.

## Why this matters

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A binomial variable counts successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with the same success probability $p$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 53: Dominated convergence combines pointwise convergence with one integrable dominating function independent of the sequence index. Week 51: A vector-valued function is differentiated by a vector limit; in finite dimension this is equivalent to differentiating coordinates. Week 46: A convergence test is chosen from the sign, comparison scale, quotient, root, or oscillation structure of the terms. Week 38: The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least degree that annihilates the endomorphism. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Probability · Binomial theorem

A binomial variable counts successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with the same success probability $p$.

### Complete worked problem

Five independent trials each succeed with probability $0.3$. Compute the probability of exactly two successes.

### Complete worked derivation

The number $X$ of successes is binomial because the number of trials is fixed, the trials are independent, and every trial has the same success probability $p=0.3$. Exactly two successes can occupy any two of the five trial positions, giving $\binom52$ choices. Each chosen pattern has probability $0.3^2 0.7^3$. Therefore

$$P(X=2)=\binom52(0.3)^2(0.7)^3=10(0.09)(0.343)=0.3087.$$

The combinatorial factor and the common pattern probability account for all disjoint cases.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

If trial success probabilities differ, or if trials are dependent, the common factor $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ is no longer valid. The count of successes is then not modeled by this binomial law.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

content.title: Week 54, day 3: Construct a proof
content.markdown: You are in **MP**. This page follows the week 54 syllabus requirement: Countable probability and standard discrete laws.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can write a complete proof of this exact target: prove that the geometric masses sum to one.

## Why this matters

This is the week's central reasoning target: Prove that the geometric masses sum to one.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values with total $1$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 53: Dominated convergence combines pointwise convergence with one integrable dominating function independent of the sequence index. Week 51: A vector-valued function is differentiated by a vector limit; in finite dimension this is equivalent to differentiating coordinates. Week 46: A convergence test is chosen from the sign, comparison scale, quotient, root, or oscillation structure of the terms. Week 38: The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least degree that annihilates the endomorphism. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove that the geometric masses sum to one.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: the probability of a complement

Let $A$ be an event. The events $A$ and $A^c$ are disjoint and their union is the full sample space $\Omega$.

Finite additivity therefore gives $P(A)+P(A^c)=P(\Omega)=1$. Rearranging yields $P(A^c)=1-P(A)$.

**Why the proof is complete.** It names the disjoint union that permits addition, invokes the probability axiom, and only then rearranges.

### Week 54 analogous target

### Complete task packet



**Exact task.** Prove that the geometric masses sum to one.

**Definition available for this task.** A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values with total $1$.

**Concrete example available for comparison.** $P(X=k)=2^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$ is a law because the geometric sum equals $1$.

**Boundary that must be checked.** Point masses whose series diverges or sums below $1$ do not define the stated full law.

## Use the feedback

Read the earliest important issue first. Rewrite that step before continuing. Keep every part that the review identifies as correct.

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** A Poisson variable with parameter $\lambda>0$ has $P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$.

**Worked example to compare:** Its expectation and variance both equal $\lambda$.

**Boundary to compare:** A Poisson variable has unbounded countable support, unlike a binomial variable.

### Week 53 — Parameter-dependent integrals · Integral

**Definition.** Continuity of a parameter integral follows by combining pointwise continuity in the parameter with an integrable local domination.

**Example.** $F(x)=\int_0^1e^{-xt}dt$ is continuous for $x\ge0$ by domination with $1$.

**Boundary.** Pointwise continuity of the integrand is not enough on an improper domain without domination.

**Proof target.** Prove continuity of a parameter integral using a stated domination theorem.

**Decisive proof route.** If $f(t,x)$ is continuous in $t$ and dominated by an integrable $g(x)$ near $t_0$, then $f(t,x)\to f(t_0,x)$ pointwise. Dominated convergence moves the limit through the integral, proving continuity.

### Week 51 — Vector-valued functions · Taylor

**Definition.** Taylor's formula for a vector-valued function applies componentwise with a vector remainder estimate.

**Example.** $r(t+h)=r(t)+hr'(t)+O(h^2)$ for a twice differentiable plane curve.

**Boundary.** A componentwise expansion needs one remainder control valid for the chosen vector norm.

**Proof target.** Prove that the derivative of a constant-norm curve is orthogonal to the position vector.

**Decisive proof route.** Differentiate $\langle\gamma(t),\gamma(t)\rangle=c^2$. The product rule gives $2\langle\gamma'(t),\gamma(t)\rangle=0$, so velocity is orthogonal to position.

### Week 46 — Numerical series · Remainder

**Definition.** The remainder after $n$ terms is the tail $R_n=\sum_{k>n}u_k$, estimated with a theorem suited to the terms.

**Example.** For a positive decreasing function, integral comparison bounds the series tail by neighboring improper integrals.

**Boundary.** A remainder estimate must control the full infinite tail, not only the next term unless an alternating-series theorem applies.

**Proof target.** Prove an integral-comparison bound for a positive decreasing series.

**Decisive proof route.** For positive decreasing $f$ with $u_n=f(n)$, compare each rectangle with the integrals on $[n,n+1]$. Summing gives the two-sided bounds between the series tail and adjacent improper-integral tails.

### Week 38 — Linear maps · Kernel decomposition

**Definition.** If coprime polynomials $P_i$ satisfy $\prod P_i(T)=0$, the space decomposes as the direct sum of the kernels $\ker P_i(T)$.

**Example.** Distinct eigenvalue factors give the direct sum of their generalized eigenspaces.

**Boundary.** Coprimality is essential; overlapping factors do not give the same direct-sum conclusion.

**Proof target.** Prove the two-factor kernel decomposition when the annihilating factors are coprime.

**Decisive proof route.** If $P$ and $Q$ are coprime and $P(T)Q(T)=0$, choose $A P+B Q=1$. Then every $x$ decomposes as $B(T)Q(T)x+A(T)P(T)x$, lying in $\ker P(T)$ and $\ker Q(T)$ respectively. Their intersection is zero by the same identity.

**Scheduled review answer key.**

### Week 53 — Parameter-dependent integrals · Integral

**Definition.** Continuity of a parameter integral follows by combining pointwise continuity in the parameter with an integrable local domination.

**Example.** $F(x)=\int_0^1e^{-xt}dt$ is continuous for $x\ge0$ by domination with $1$.

**Boundary.** Pointwise continuity of the integrand is not enough on an improper domain without domination.

**Proof target.** Prove continuity of a parameter integral using a stated domination theorem.

**Decisive proof route.** If $f(t,x)$ is continuous in $t$ and dominated by an integrable $g(x)$ near $t_0$, then $f(t,x)\to f(t_0,x)$ pointwise. Dominated convergence moves the limit through the integral, proving continuity.

### Week 51 — Vector-valued functions · Taylor

**Definition.** Taylor's formula for a vector-valued function applies componentwise with a vector remainder estimate.

**Example.** $r(t+h)=r(t)+hr'(t)+O(h^2)$ for a twice differentiable plane curve.

**Boundary.** A componentwise expansion needs one remainder control valid for the chosen vector norm.

**Proof target.** Prove that the derivative of a constant-norm curve is orthogonal to the position vector.

**Decisive proof route.** Differentiate $\langle\gamma(t),\gamma(t)\rangle=c^2$. The product rule gives $2\langle\gamma'(t),\gamma(t)\rangle=0$, so velocity is orthogonal to position.

### Week 46 — Numerical series · Remainder

**Definition.** The remainder after $n$ terms is the tail $R_n=\sum_{k>n}u_k$, estimated with a theorem suited to the terms.

**Example.** For a positive decreasing function, integral comparison bounds the series tail by neighboring improper integrals.

**Boundary.** A remainder estimate must control the full infinite tail, not only the next term unless an alternating-series theorem applies.

**Proof target.** Prove an integral-comparison bound for a positive decreasing series.

**Decisive proof route.** For positive decreasing $f$ with $u_n=f(n)$, compare each rectangle with the integrals on $[n,n+1]$. Summing gives the two-sided bounds between the series tail and adjacent improper-integral tails.

### Week 38 — Linear maps · Kernel decomposition

**Definition.** If coprime polynomials $P_i$ satisfy $\prod P_i(T)=0$, the space decomposes as the direct sum of the kernels $\ker P_i(T)$.

**Example.** Distinct eigenvalue factors give the direct sum of their generalized eigenspaces.

**Boundary.** Coprimality is essential; overlapping factors do not give the same direct-sum conclusion.

**Proof target.** Prove the two-factor kernel decomposition when the annihilating factors are coprime.

**Decisive proof route.** If $P$ and $Q$ are coprime and $P(T)Q(T)=0$, choose $A P+B Q=1$. Then every $x$ decomposes as $B(T)Q(T)x+A(T)P(T)x$, lying in $\ker P(T)$ and $\ker Q(T)$ respectively. Their intersection is zero by the same identity.

## Define the objects in independent families, expectation, variance, and covariance

A family is mutually independent when every finite subfamily has product probabilities for all corresponding events.

### A complete first example

Independent coordinate variables on a product probability space form an independent family.

content.markdown: You are in **MP**. This page follows the week 55 syllabus requirement: Independent families, expectation, variance, and covariance.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can apply a definition-first method to a complete Probability · First absolute moment verification and check its boundary.

## Why this matters

A stable route lets you decide what to do before calculation begins. The same route will support tomorrow's proof and the later timed transfer.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: $L^1$ consists of integrable random variables with $E[|X|]<\infty$. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 54: A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values whose total is $1$. Week 52: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals near an infinite endpoint or singularity. Week 47: Uniform convergence means one index works for every point: $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$. Week 39: The adjoint $u^*$ is defined by $\langle u(x),y\rangle=\langle x,u^*(y)\rangle$ for all $x,y$. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Follow a reliable method



**Deliberate method replay.** The definition is repeated exactly so that every decision in the new worked problem can be checked against it. The worked problem, formative checkpoint, and exit task are three different mathematical cases.

Use this route before trying shortcuts:

1. Name the objects, domains, and requested conclusion.

2. Write the definition or theorem that can produce that conclusion.

3. Check its hypotheses against the data.

4. Calculate one justified line at a time.

5. Test the result against a simple or boundary case.

### Exact definition or theorem: Probability · First absolute moment

$L^1$ consists of integrable random variables with $E[|X|]<\infty$.

### Complete worked problem

Let $X$ be a real random variable with $E[X^2]=9$. Prove that $X\in L^1$ and give a numerical bound for $E[|X|]$.

### Complete worked derivation

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the random variables $|X|$ and $1$:

$$E[|X|]=E[|X|\cdot1]\le\sqrt{E[X^2]}\sqrt{E[1^2]}.$$

Because $E[X^2]=9$ and $E[1]=1$, this gives

$$E[|X|]\le3<\infty.$$

Thus $X$ is absolutely integrable and belongs to $L^1$. The second-moment hypothesis supplies more than a merely formal signed expectation.

### Boundary and failed hypothesis

Symmetric cancellation does not prove integrability. Normalize probabilities proportional to $1/n^2$ at both $n$ and $-n$ for $n\ge1$. Symmetric truncated signed sums cancel, but $E[|X|]$ contains a divergent harmonic sum, so the integrable expectation $E[X]$ is not defined.

The solution and the boundary check concern different mathematical cases. The solution above is the fully displayed model; the checkpoint below asks you to begin a new case rather than repeat it.

The formative checkpoint asks only for the first justified check on that different case. After feedback, the exit activity asks you to repair and verify it completely.

## Build a proof before writing it



Today's independent target is to prove variance additivity for two independent square-integrable variables.

Separate the work into four boxes: assumptions, target, definitions to expand, and earlier results you may invoke. Then draw a short arrow from each assumption to the step where it is first used.

### Complete model proof: the probability of a complement

Let $A$ be an event. The events $A$ and $A^c$ are disjoint and their union is the full sample space $\Omega$.

Finite additivity therefore gives $P(A)+P(A^c)=P(\Omega)=1$. Rearranging yields $P(A^c)=1-P(A)$.

**Why the proof is complete.** It names the disjoint union that permits addition, invokes the probability axiom, and only then rearranges.

## Use the feedback

## Open the record after retrieval

**Definition to compare:** $L^2$ consists of square-integrable random variables with $E[X^2]<\infty$.

**Worked example to compare:** Variance is finite for every $L^2$ variable.

**Boundary to compare:** Being in $L^1$ does not imply being in $L^2$.

### Week 54 — Probability · Countable

**Definition.** A countable discrete law assigns nonnegative masses to countably many values with total $1$.

**Example.** $P(X=k)=2^{-k}$ for $k\ge1$ is a law because the geometric sum equals $1$.

**Boundary.** Point masses whose series diverges or sums below $1$ do not define the stated full law.

**Proof target.** Prove that the geometric masses sum to one.

**Decisive proof route.** For geometric law $P(X=k)=p(1-p)^{k-1}$ on $k\ge1$, the total mass is $p\sum_{j\ge0}(1-p)^j=p/p=1$ because $0<p\le1$.

### Week 52 — Improper integrals · Parts

**Definition.** Integration by parts for an improper integral is performed on finite truncations before passing to the limit.

**Example.** $\int_1^R(\log x)/x^2dx$ is integrated by parts first, then $R\to\infty$.

**Boundary.** The limiting boundary term must exist; formal endpoint notation cannot replace that check.

**Proof target.** Prove the $p$-integral convergence criterion by evaluating finite truncations.

**Decisive proof route.** For $p\ne1$, $\int_1^R x^{-p}dx=(R^{1-p}-1)/(1-p)$, whose limit is finite exactly when $p>1$. For $p=1$, the truncation is $\log R\to\infty$.

### Week 47 — Sequences of functions · Uniform

**Definition.** $f_n\to f$ uniformly when $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$.

**Example.** $x/n\to0$ uniformly on $[0,1]$ because the supremum error is $1/n$.

**Boundary.** Pointwise convergence to a discontinuous limit on a compact interval cannot be uniform when all $f_n$ are continuous.

**Proof target.** Prove that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

**Decisive proof route.** Given $f_n\to f$ uniformly and $x\to a$, choose $n$ so $\|f-f_n\|_\infty<\varepsilon/3$, then use continuity of $f_n$ at $a$. The triangle inequality splits $|f(x)-f(a)|$ into three terms below $\varepsilon/3$.

### Week 39 — Euclidean spaces · Isometry

**Definition.** A linear isometry preserves norms, equivalently inner products in a real Euclidean space.

**Example.** Reflections and rotations are linear isometries.

**Boundary.** A general affine isometry may include a translation and therefore need not be linear.

**Proof target.** Prove that a linear map is an isometry exactly when $u^*u=I$.

**Decisive proof route.** The norm identity $\|ux\|^2=\langle u^*ux,x\rangle$ shows that $u^*u=I$ implies isometry. Conversely, preserving norms and polarizing gives $\langle ux,uy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$, hence $u^*u=I$.

content.title: Week 56, day 1: Build the foundation
content.markdown: You are in **MP**. This page follows the week 56 syllabus requirement: Generating functions and concentration inequalities.

## Today's learning goal

By the end of this page, you can state the defining conditions for Probability · Probability-generating functions, verify the supplied example, and identify why the boundary case fails.

## Why this matters

Definitions control every later method. Naming each condition now prevents familiar notation from concealing a false assumption.

## What you need first

The exact current definition is: The probability generating function of a nonnegative integer-valued variable is $G_X(s)=E[s^X]$ on its domain. The scheduled prerequisite statements are: Week 55: A family is mutually independent when every finite subfamily has product probabilities for intersections. Week 53: Dominated convergence combines pointwise convergence with one integrable dominating function independent of the sequence index. Week 48: Normal convergence means the sup norms of the terms form a convergent numerical series; it implies uniform convergence. Week 40: A self-adjoint map satisfies $u=u^*$. In finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces it has an orthonormal eigenbasis. If any statement or symbol is unfamiliar, stop and open the linked concept before attempting the checkpoint.

## Define the objects in generating functions and concentration inequalities

The probability generating function of a nonnegative integer-valued variable is $G_X(s)=E[s^X]$ on its domain.

### A complete first example

For a Poisson variable, $G_X(s)=e^{\lambda(s-1)}$.

The example works because it meets the definition above. Name each condition before calculating; this prevents a familiar-looking expression from being used outside its domain.

### Boundary case to remember

Differentiating at $1$ requires the corresponding moment to be finite and the operation justified.
